entries.title: Anthropic's unreleased model built five attack chains against major software
entries.summary: Anthropic used an unreleased internal research model to find and chain vulnerabilities in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows and Linux. The results included a one-click Chrome sandbox escape (62 CVEs patched in Chrome 156), a Safari same-origin policy bypass, an Android lock screen bypass, a remote Windows QUIC crash (CVE-2026-33096) and a zero-click Linux multipath TCP root exploit (CVE-2026-98432). Anthropic calls two of its lessons particularly important: run many different scanning agents in parallel, and scan at pull-request time to stop new bugs.

lessons.point: Running more compute and a wider mix of scanning strategies finds substantially more vulnerabilities than a single scanner.
lessons.excerpt: Test-time compute scaling and scanner diversity substantially increase how many vulnerabilities you find.

lessons.point: Judge each scanner by how many new findings it adds to the combined set, not by its raw count.
lessons.excerpt: measures each scanner by how many additional vulnerabilities it contributes to the mix

lessons.point: Model-built chains can combine intended behaviors that are harmless on their own into a full exploit, as in the data-only Safari chain.
lessons.excerpt: Several of the weaknesses are not vulnerabilities on their own but intended behaviors that become exploitable when combined.

lessons.point: Clearing the existing backlog is not enough. Scanning at pull-request time cuts the rate at which new bugs enter the code.
lessons.excerpt: For that, we recommend scanning at PR time.

entries.takeaway: Frontier models now build working multi-bug exploit chains against hardened targets with little human help, so defenders need to scan their own code at scale and at PR time.

actionable.title: Run diverse parallel scanning agents behind one verification pipeline
actionable.detail: Run several scanner strategies in parallel: per-function coverage ('is there a vulnerability in this function?'), goal-based ('could anything here compromise customer data?') and threat-model-based ('does anything bypass the documented threat model?'). Track coverage so the whole codebase gets processed. Score each scanner by the unique findings it adds. Run variant analysis on every confirmed bug. Send every finding through one shared verification and risk-rating step so new scanners do not lower the quality bar. Add a PR-time security check, such as Anthropic's public security-guidance Claude Code plugin.

entries.prior_art: Closest pool entries: 'Claude found 493 attack-surface issues across 25 open-source projects' (finds issues but builds no exploit chains), 'GitHub Security Lab found 24 Android vulnerabilities with its AI agent', and the Mythos 5 AISI incident (a cyber-capability incident, not vulnerability research). New here: end-to-end exploit chains against Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows and Linux.
entries.threat: Frontier models can now discover and chain several vulnerabilities into working one-click or zero-click exploits against browsers, phones and kernels, work that used to need specialist teams.
entries.conditions: An attacker needs a model with comparable capability and code, binaries or a live device to analyze. The Linux exploit also needs a reachable multipath TCP listener, and the Windows crash needs a native HTTP/3 (QUIC) listener.
entries.mitigations: Apply the Chrome 156, Apple, Android, Windows (CVE-2026-33096) and Linux kernel (CVE-2026-98432) fixes, scan your own code with diverse AI scanners plus variant analysis, and add security scanning at pull-request time.

entries.title: Atlassian CVE-2026-21589 is a pre-auth file read in Data Center products
entries.summary: The shared atlassian-plugins-webresource library (vulnerable 6.0.7, changed in 6.0.8) turns '::' into '/' after path checks, so a request like /download/resources/<plugin>/images/..::..::WEB-INF::web.xml reads any file inside the Tomcat webapp without logging in. watchTowr reproduced it on Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket. Where Jira is integrated with Crowd, WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties holds the Crowd application password in plaintext, which lets an attacker create a user and add it to jira-administrators.
entries.takeaway: Patch every Atlassian Data Center product now; if you use Crowd, also rotate the Crowd application passwords and restrict Crowd by IP allowlist.

lessons.point: The root cause is a custom path escape: the router decodes '::' to '/' after traversal checks, so '..::' is a traversal primitive that generic filters miss.
lessons.excerpt: These functions match and replace double colons (`::`) with forward slashes (`/`).

lessons.point: Impact is bounded to the webapp root, not the whole filesystem, so severity depends on what config lives in WEB-INF.
lessons.excerpt: While we are not able to traverse outside of the Tomcat context, we discovered it is possible to read any file within the application server itself.

lessons.point: The documented Crowd integration stores a plaintext app password in a file the bug can read, turning file read into identity-provider admin.
lessons.excerpt: The Crowd config file is located at `WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties`.

lessons.point: Crowd app credentials grant user creation and group changes across the Atlassian stack.
lessons.excerpt: When you access Atlassian Crowd directly with the leaked credentials, it is basically game over.

actionable.title: Patch Atlassian Data Center and rotate Crowd app credentials
actionable.detail: Upgrade to the fixed versions (e.g. Jira Software 9.12.40/10.3.26/11.3.12, Confluence 9.2.26/10.2.19, Bitbucket 9.4.26/10.2.8/10.5.1, Crowd 6.3.7+). Until patched, apply Atlassian's advisory WAF regex, which blocks '..' next to '/', backslash, '::' or their percent-encodings. Search access logs for download/resources requests containing '..::'. If any exposed instance uses Crowd, rotate the application.password in crowd.properties and restrict Crowd's remote-address allowlist. watchTowr's detection generator is at github.com/watchtowrlabs/watchTowr-vs-Atlassian-CVE-2026-21589.

entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim. Verifier: the check-then-unescape ordering is inferred; the Crowd chain needs network reach to Crowd (an IP allowlist may block it). Verifier novelty 70; kept 68.
entries.prior_art: Closest pool entry is SecurityWeek's routine Atlassian October 2026 third-party CVE bulletin; this is a separate first-party critical bug with root cause, routes, and a file-read-to-admin chain. It echoes earlier Atlassian pre-auth file-read bugs, but the '::' slash-escape primitive in the shared web-resource library is specific to this case.
entries.threat: Unauthenticated read of any file in the application webroot, including WEB-INF config; with Crowd integration, leaked app credentials allow creating admin users.
entries.conditions: Network-reachable Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Software/JSM, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible or Fisheye Data Center below the fixed versions; Crowd takeover additionally needs crowd.properties in WEB-INF and network reach to Crowd.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to Atlassian's fixed versions; apply the advisory WAF rule meanwhile; rotate Crowd application passwords; IP-restrict Crowd; hunt logs for '..::' in download/resources paths.

entries.title: Claude found 493 attack-surface issues across 25 open-source projects
entries.summary: Anthropic ran Claude over 25 open-source projects (over five million lines) to find code reachable without need, rather than individual bugs. It found 493 issues, including 94 configuration combinations that silently turned off a security control, and a pattern in four projects where hostname-based deny rules fail open when reverse DNS lookups are off. In OpenSSH, about 4,500 lines of ML-DSA-44 post-quantum code were reachable before authentication even when the algorithm was disabled; after several rounds of fixes, OpenSSH 10.6 checks the allow lists before parsing.

lessons.point: Option combinations are a large blind spot: many were accepted silently and undocumented.
lessons.excerpt: Claude found 162 security sensitive configuration combinations that were accepted both without an error or warning and without any documentation of the expected behavior of their interaction.

lessons.point: sshd parsed attacker-chosen key types before checking whether they were allowed.
lessons.excerpt: The daemon parsed whichever key type the client sent, (and, for certificates, it also verified the embedded CA signature). Only then did it check whether that key type was allowed.

lessons.point: Hostname deny rules compared against a bare IP never match, so the list fails open.
lessons.excerpt: This means that a deny rule would never fire, and the list would fail open.

lessons.point: For the default-configuration pass, a gate is accepted only when the project's own tests give identical results.
lessons.excerpt: it requires modified builds to have identical results.

entries.takeaway: Cutting pre-auth and default-reachable code lowers the severity of bugs you have not found, and an LLM can do this audit at scale.

actionable.title: Run a three-pass attack-surface reduction review with an LLM
actionable.detail: In fresh contexts, have the model (1) inventory entry points reachable in the default config that no intended feature uses, (2) list parsing or state recorded before auth or protocol state transitions, and (3) enumerate security-relevant option pairs that silently disable or weaken a control; confirm each with a dynamic trace, and accept a gate only if the project's test suite gives identical results.

entries.prior_art: Pool entries on frontier-model vulnerability discovery (Mythos-era bug finding, AI-built PHP pre-auth chains) and classic attack-surface reduction guidance; this shifts from finding individual bugs to systematic reachability and config-interaction reduction with measured results and an upstream OpenSSH fix. Verifier: Attack-surface reduction (Howard/Manadhata attack-surface metrics, OpenSSH privsep and pre-auth minimization) is classic, and Anthropic's prior LLM vuln-finding posts (Firefox, OSS-Scanner) cover LLM bug finding. What is new is LLM-driven reachability and config-interaction auditing at scale, with the concrete OpenSSH 10.6 pre-auth fix.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: Complex, memory-unsafe or security-sensitive code reachable by unauthenticated clients, and configuration combinations that silently disable controls administrators believe are on.
entries.conditions: Default configurations exposing unused features, checks that run after parsing, and option pairs accepted without warnings, such as hostname deny rules with reverse DNS off or certificate requirements dropped by a conflicting option.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade OpenSSH to 10.6; check allow lists before deserialization; reject conflicting security options at config load; use IP-based access rules or enable DNS lookups when using hostname rules.

entries.title: Sanitized webmail CSS steals tokens and keylogs Outlook
entries.summary: Gareth Heyes chains allowed HTML/CSS features across Fastmail, Outlook, AOL/Yahoo/Gmail/ProtonMail and OpenAI's Atlas AI browser to defeat webmail CSS sanitization. Techniques include HTML labels that trigger arbitrary UI actions, invisible :before/:after content that feeds one story to the human and another to an AI browser (indirect prompt injection), attribute-selector nesting to brute-force login tokens after a paste-into-draft, CSS hotwiring to hijack any click, and a real-time keylogger via select+opacity plus Chrome interest invokers.
entries.takeaway: CSS sanitizers built as feature allow-lists are not a trust boundary; the only durable defense is strict iframe sandboxing plus killing dangerous selectors, select, and free-form image URLs.

lessons.point: Invisible :before/:after content lets an attacker present two different messages to the human and to an AI browser reading the same email, enabling indirect prompt injection through webmail.
lessons.excerpt: you could use the `:before` and `:after` pseudo-elements to hide the text from the LLM and you could use opacity to hide it from the victim. This creates a disparity between what the victim sees and what the LLM sees, potentially altering the email's context.

lessons.point: CSS attribute selectors, combined with nesting, can brute-force secret URL parameters (e.g. Medium's 12-char login token) inside a webmail draft after a single paste, without JavaScript.
lessons.excerpt: using nesting we can match the start with one selector that's outputted only once and then nest the other selectors to brute-force the token with a smaller amount of CSS

lessons.point: The only defense that actually holds is strict iframe sandboxing plus removing dangerous selectors and select elements; feature-level CSS/HTML allow lists get bypassed by gadgets and mutation.
lessons.excerpt: One of the best methods to protect against these attacks is strict isolation. If you isolate the email message using sandboxed iframes you restrict the ability to break out of trusted boundaries.

lessons.point: CSS hotwiring lets an attacker with allow-listed CSS force the victim's next click, anywhere on the page, to fire a chosen UI action, including multi-step ones.
lessons.excerpt: CSS hotwiring is a technique that allows you to force the victim to click a specific UI action when clicking anywhere on the page **including multi-step actions** using just CSS.

actionable.title: Threat-model webmail-style renderers as adversarial input surfaces for both humans and AI browsers
actionable.detail: For any product rendering third-party HTML/CSS to a user (webmail, comment systems, agent-visible pages): isolate in a sandboxed iframe; strip select and any dangerous selectors (:has, :checked, :focus, :not); route images through a proxy; reject data: URLs; and assume attackers will use :before/:after to differ human vs LLM view. Add a regression test that renders a corpus of PortSwigger's published payloads and confirms none reach the DOM.

entries.prior_art: Apple ANSI-DNS-exfil chain (embracethered) covers CLI-side prompt-injection exfil; CSS-side webmail attacks trace back to Heiderich's mutation XSS and Gerste's font-based CSS exfil. The AI-browser-via-CSS-hidden-content angle is materially new relative to the pool.
entries.threat: A single crafted email lets an attacker (a) spoof or hijack UI actions in Outlook/Fastmail via HTML labels + CSS hotwiring, (b) exfiltrate login tokens and passwords from third-party sites the victim pastes into a webmail draft, (c) inject instructions that only the AI browser sees, causing an AI email assistant to open attacker-controlled tabs and leak the victim's name, and (d) keylog Outlook via CSS/select gadgets. All from allow-listed HTML/CSS with no JavaScript.
entries.conditions: Webmail client renders untrusted HTML/CSS in the same DOM as the trusted UI (no sandboxed iframe isolation), or the user pastes clipboard HTML into a contenteditable draft on Firefox, or an AI browser (e.g. Atlas) processes the email body as prompt context.
entries.mitigations: Sandbox untrusted email content in an iframe with a strict CSP that blocks external image requests and data: URLs. Strip select, dangerous selectors (:has, :checked, :focus, :not), and image URLs pointing to attacker-controllable domains. When an image proxy is available, force all image requests through it. In AI-browser layers, treat CSS-hidden or opacity-zero content as untrusted content the model should not act on.

entries.title: watchTowr breaks PaperCut NG/MF patches again with an auth bypass plus RCE
entries.summary: PaperCut 26.0.3 was exploited in the wild through an auth bypass (CVE-2026-81578) chained with a post-auth RCE (CVE-2026-82078). The root cause is that PaperCut, built on Apache Tapestry 3, checks authorization only on the root page in the `service` parameter: `direct/1/<public page>/<private page>/<form>` reaches authenticated forms. PaperCut patched page by page, and watchTowr bypassed each fix. The final bypass (WT-2026-0143) reaches Setup Wizard forms through `Home`, resets the admin password in four POSTs, and is chained with a new Scan to Fax command-execution bug (CVE-2026-82077), fixed in 26.0.5.
entries.takeaway: When authorization is enforced per page instead of globally, patching individual pages invites repeated bypasses; PaperCut needed four patch rounds, and admins should be on 26.0.5 or later.

lessons.point: The core flaw: Tapestry lets one `service` parameter chain several pages, but PaperCut only authorized the first (root) page.
lessons.excerpt: However, the code only checks authorization for the root page, so `LogonMessage` in our case, this page does not require authentication.

lessons.point: Fixing individual pages and forms instead of adding a global authorization check left other reachable forms, like the Setup Wizard, unprotected.
lessons.excerpt: Still, without a global authorization check implemented for all pages, it is hard to keep track and manually verify every page in the codebase.

lessons.point: Routing setup forms through `Home` skips their own guard, so the 'setup already completed' flag never stops an attacker from re-running setup and resetting the admin password.
lessons.excerpt: Setup pages `pageValidate` method will never be called (thanks to the bypass), so the `system.setup-completed` value is irrelevant for the attacker.

lessons.point: PaperCut assigned fewer CVEs than distinct bugs, folding patch bypasses into existing IDs, so CVE-based tracking undercounts the fix rounds needed.
lessons.excerpt: due to PaperCut bundling vulnerabilities and then patch bypasses for those same vulnerabilities into singular CVE IDs

actionable.title: Get PaperCut NG/MF to 26.0.5+ and check for setup-wizard abuse
actionable.detail: Upgrade PaperCut NG/MF to 26.0.5 or later (26.0.4 and 26.0.4-PO builds 76508/76530 are each still bypassable for part of the chain). Check app logs for `service=direct/1/Home/Setup` or `direct/1/LogonMessage/` style multi-page requests, unexpected admin password changes, and changes to scan-to-fax command settings. Keep the admin interface off the internet.

entries.verify_note: All four excerpts verbatim; ids and patch rounds match the source. Verifier novelty 65.
entries.prior_art: watchTowr's SolarWinds Web Help Desk chain (WebObjects multi-step auth bypasses) and the earlier PaperCut KEV bugs CVE-2023-27350/27351. This adds a concrete legacy-framework pattern (Tapestry 3 multi-page `service` routing skipping per-page auth) plus a documented series of per-page patches failing in sequence.
entries.threat: Unauthenticated attacker resets the PaperCut admin password via re-run setup forms, then executes OS commands through admin functionality (Scan to Fax command path).
entries.conditions: PaperCut NG/MF up to 26.0.4-PO build 76508 for the WT-2026-0143 plus CVE-2026-82077 chain; 26.0.3 for the in-the-wild chain; web interface reachable by the attacker.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to 26.0.5 or later; restrict the admin web interface to trusted networks; apply PaperCut's IOCs and hunt for multi-page `service` requests and unexpected admin credential changes.

entries.title: Trojanized Claude Code extension on Cursor Marketplace plants persistent SSH backdoor
entries.summary: Phorion found that Claude Code for VS Code version 2.1.313 on the Cursor Marketplace carried injected code. The code runs as soon as the extension file loads, appends an attacker key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys and opens a reverse SSH tunnel to 134.209.82.225. It also sets up persistence on macOS, Linux and Windows and sends a report on the host back to the operator. That report includes the names, but not the values, of environment variables that look like secrets. A bug in the macOS check often stops it from turning on SSH, but the key and persistence still get installed, and removing the extension does not remove them.

lessons.point: The payload is an immediately invoked function prepended to extension.js. It runs when Node loads the module, before activate(), and needs no user action.
lessons.excerpt: executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal `activate` callback even runs

lessons.point: Rules that only watch processes miss this, because the key is written with Node's fs API rather than shell tools. Defenders need file telemetry that flags IDE helper processes writing to authorized_keys.
lessons.excerpt: process-only rules watching for shell commands like `echo` or `tee` touching `authorized_keys` won’t catch it

lessons.point: Hunt by key fingerprint, not by the 'svc-telemetry' comment, because the malware itself only checks the comment string.
lessons.excerpt: When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.

lessons.point: Uninstalling the extension does not clean up. Responders must kill the tunnel loop, remove the LaunchAgent, cron or scheduled-task persistence, remove the planted key and rotate credentials.
lessons.excerpt: uninstalling the extension alone won’t remove the backdoor

entries.takeaway: An AI coding-assistant extension from the official vendor, served by an editor marketplace, ran with full user rights when loaded, so hunt for integrated development environment (IDE) extension hosts writing to ~/.ssh and LaunchAgents and do not treat uninstalling as remediation.

actionable.title: Hunt for and clean up Claude Code 2.1.313 extension backdoor artifacts
actionable.detail: Across the fleet, look for anthropic.claude-code-2.1.313 extension directories. Search authorized_keys for the key fingerprint SHA256:0Z6R+DF64Do2nwQic8a7kkfDLNNk4IiK+2U2Rci4htk, not just the svc-telemetry comment. Look for ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist, ~/.config/.smt and ~/.config/.smtk, $TMPDIR/.stk_* files, ssh or autossh running with '-R *:0:localhost:22', and traffic to 134.209.82.225 on port 22 or 8099. Add an EDR rule for Code Helper or Cursor Helper processes writing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or creating com.apple.* LaunchAgents. Check SSH logs for logins from localhost using that key, then rotate credentials if any are found.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: all four lessons and the IOCs supported by the Phorion writeup (port 8099 is the beacon port). Novelty lowered to the verifier's 55.
entries.prior_art: The nearest pool entries are archive 'Cursor's VS Code import drops extension versions and installs latest' (Open VSX identity and versions), archive 'Markdown Preview Enhanced, a VS Code extension, chained flaws into RCE' and product-security 'OVHcloud CLI GitHub releases carried attacker binaries ... GlassWorm'. None covers a trojanized official AI coding-assistant extension with this kind of detection detail.
entries.threat: A backdoored official Claude Code extension bundle (2.1.313) on the Cursor Marketplace runs a payload when the module loads. The payload plants an attacker SSH key, opens a reverse SSH tunnel to 134.209.82.225 for interactive access, persists through a LaunchAgent, cron job or scheduled task, and reports host details and the names of secret-looking environment variables.
entries.conditions: A developer installs or auto-updates to Claude Code for VS Code 2.1.313 from the Cursor Marketplace. Full inbound access on macOS also needs Remote Login (SSH) to be already on or turned on later, or passwordless sudo.
entries.mitigations: Find and remove 2.1.313. Kill the tunnel processes. Remove com.apple.sysmond.plist, the @reboot cron entry or the SysMon task and Startup script, and the ~/.config/.smt, .smtk and /tmp/.stk_* files. Remove the svc-telemetry key and confirm Remote Login is off. Rotate credentials if SSH was on or an inbound login appears. Alert on IDE extension hosts modifying ~/.ssh.
entries.author: _chall

editorial.reason: A trojanized official AI coding-assistant extension, covered by six outlets, with concrete hunting steps (key fingerprint, persistence paths, an EDR rule) and the lesson that uninstalling does not remediate.

entries.title: pwn.ai found a new Linux networking bug class escaping KVM guests
entries.summary: pwn.ai researchers, working in Vercel's sandbox challenge, found that guest-controlled checksum metadata can rewrite an IPv4 header after the host kernel has validated it. The bug is in Linux networking, not in KVM itself, so many hypervisors are affected. In their lab they turned a memory disclosure into selected 64-byte host-kernel writes and a host-root helper run. They credit GPT-5.6 Sol as the main reasoning engine inside a long-running research harness. The upstream fix validates checksum_start before completing the checksum.

lessons.point: The authors call it a new class: untrusted checksum metadata edits packet fields after validation.
lessons.excerpt: untrusted checksum metadata can rewrite security-sensitive packet fields after the kernel has already validated and acted on them

lessons.point: The bug is outside the hypervisor, so KVM-only audits miss it.
lessons.excerpt: the vulnerability wasn't even in the hypervisor, it was in the Linux networking stack.

lessons.point: An LLM provided source-level analysis within a human-directed harness.
lessons.excerpt: served as the primary reasoning engine for source-level analysis, exploring attack paths, and challenging assumptions

lessons.point: The accepted fix validates the checksum start.
lessons.excerpt: ipv4: validate checksum_start before completing checksum

entries.takeaway: VM isolation depends on the kernel's networking code, so patch KVM hosts and sandbox providers.

actionable.title: Patch hypervisor hosts and sandbox providers
actionable.detail: Apply the kernel fix on every KVM host (and nested or microVM sandboxes), and ask your sandbox provider for their patch status; treat guest-originated packet metadata as untrusted in custom kernels.

entries.prior_art: Earlier VM-escape work targets hypervisor device emulation; this reaches the host through guest-controlled metadata in core networking, with LLM-assisted discovery. Verifier: Checksum offload/virtio_net metadata bugs (virtio-net GSO/csum handling fixes); Google Big Sleep and XBOW LLM-driven vuln finds; kvmCTF KVM escapes
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; discrepancies it found (title/summary overstatements) were corrected before merge.

entries.title: Claude wrote machine-checked no-crash proofs for 239 OSS-Fuzz entry points
entries.author: Keane Lucas et al. (Anthropic, Theorem)
entries.summary: Anthropic and Theorem had Claude prove, in Rocq, that 239 OSS-Fuzz entry points in 123 open-source libraries never crash (no memory-safety error or failed assertion) for any input up to 64 MB, after patching the bugs it found along the way. The spec is derived mechanically from the existing fuzz harness plus formal RISC-V and Linux-process semantics, so the ~180M lines of proof need no human review: trust reduces to the semantics, the theorem statements and the Rocq checker. Scope is narrow (single-threaded static RISC-V binaries, fixed memory budget) and compute is large, but it moves formal verification from niche to a pipeline step.

lessons.point: LLM-written formal proofs now scale to production libraries at the binary level, not just toy programs.
lessons.excerpt: proved that there are no crashes on any input (up to 64 MB) for 239 entry points across 123 different OSS-Fuzz libraries

lessons.point: The spec problem is sidestepped by reusing what developers already wrote: an existing fuzz harness becomes the property to prove.
lessons.excerpt: automatically converting their preexisting compilable test suites into a spec

lessons.point: Machine checking replaces review of the AI output: the trusted base is the semantics, the theorem statements and the checker, not the 600k-line proofs.
lessons.excerpt: virtually none of it needs to be manually reviewed

lessons.point: The guarantee is scoped: it holds only for single-threaded static RISC-V binaries on Linux under a memory budget, and bugs may remain in the trusted components.
lessons.excerpt: assume that the program runs as a single-threaded static binary with a fixed memory budget on a RISC-V CPU using Linux OS

lessons.point: Attempting proofs is itself a bug finder: failures pointed at real bugs that fuzzing had missed.
lessons.excerpt: the process of attempting to prove these specs discovered hundreds of bugs

entries.threat: AI-accelerated bug discovery and exploit chaining outpacing test-based assurance for memory-unsafe code.
entries.conditions: C/C++ libraries with existing fuzz harnesses; proofs currently limited to single-threaded static RISC-V Linux binaries.
entries.mitigations: Turn fuzz harnesses into no-crash specs and have an LLM produce checker-verified proofs; review the theorem statements and trusted semantics rather than proof text.
entries.takeaway: If you maintain C/C++ with fuzz harnesses, those harnesses are now candidate proof specs: an LLM plus a proof checker can turn 'fuzzed a lot' into 'proved no crash' for the covered scope.

actionable.title: Fuzz-harness-to-proof pipeline
actionable.detail: For a C/C++ library already in OSS-Fuzz, try Theorem's published add-project Claude skill and pipeline on one entry point; review only the generated theorem statement and assumptions, and treat proof failures as bug reports.

entries.prior_art: seL4 and CompCert (human-written verification at 10x code effort), binary-level verifiers like Alive2, LLM proof assistants (Baldur, AlphaProof), and AI bug finding (Big Sleep, AIxCC). None showed LLM-written, machine-checked binary-level proofs at this scale.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all excerpts verbatim; novelty 78 vs 75 (kept 75); relevance 72; noted trusted components may hold bugs and the compute cost is large.

entries.title: Wiz turned PHP memory bugs into unauthenticated RCE on WordPress using AI
entries.summary: Wiz Research reported memory-safety bugs in the PHP engine itself (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, up to CVSS 9.2), so every PHP version back to 5.4 is hit by at least one of them. The bugs sit in how PHP handles fatal errors such as out-of-memory, so a hello-world app is exposed. The bugs had existed for years; frontier models made the multi-step exploit chain practical to build and adapt per target in hours. PHP shipped the patch on October 21, 2026.

lessons.point: The bugs are in core PHP, so every app on an affected version is exposed, including a plain Hello World app.
lessons.excerpt: Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4.

lessons.point: The root cause is stale internal state left behind after fatal errors such as out-of-memory, which a later request or worker reuses.
lessons.excerpt: All of the disclosed vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues that stem from bugs in how PHP handles fatal errors while processing requests, particularly out-of-memory errors.

lessons.point: Frontier models made the exploit chain practical: they adapted exploits to different targets in hours.
lessons.excerpt: Frontier models were critical to making this process practical, enabling us to develop and adapt working exploits across multiple applications in hours.

lessons.point: Exploit complexity may no longer be a reliable barrier, so old memory bugs deserve faster patching.
lessons.excerpt: As the time and expertise required for this work decrease, complexity may no longer provide a meaningful barrier, changing how we define what is vulnerable in practice.

entries.takeaway: Patch PHP now: the flaws are in the engine, not your app, and AI has cut the cost of turning old memory bugs into working exploits.

actionable.title: Patch PHP and inventory PHP runtimes
actionable.detail: Upgrade every PHP runtime to the October 21, 2026 release, including PHP bundled in container images. If you cannot patch yet, apply your WAF or CDN vendor's PHP2Shell rule as a stopgap and treat memory disclosure as a credential-rotation trigger on exposed hosts.

entries.prior_art: Core-language RCE disclosures exist (for example PHP-CGI), but a core PHP memory-corruption chain exploited pre-auth across three CMSs with frontier-model-built exploits has no equal in the pools. Verifier: Google Big Sleep / Project Zero AI-found bugs, DARPA AIxCC, XBOW; earlier frontier-model exploit-development reports. Delta is AI-built multi-bug chain on core
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; discrepancies it found (title/summary overstatements) were corrected before merge.

editorial.reason: Core PHP RCE chain built with frontier AI; patched October 21 with broad vendor mitigations.

entries.title: PortSwigger's Gareth Heyes bypassed six of eight popular vector-image sanitizers
entries.summary: Gareth Heyes tested eight sanitizers for Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) uploads and bypassed six, using tricks such as switching one element's namespace to XHTML, animating a link into a JavaScript URL, and pointing a stylesheet instruction at a data URL. He also showed Firefox running JavaScript from a stylesheet delivered in a `Link` response header over a harmless XML body, and Safari importing a GIF as SVG through `<use>`. DOMPurify and darylldoyle/svg-sanitizer resisted every technique.

lessons.point: Two libraries held up against every technique in the post.
lessons.excerpt: Both DOMPurify and darylldoyle/svg-sanitizer held up against everything in this post, which is quite impressive.

lessons.point: A namespace switch on one element brings HTML into an SVG without foreignObject.
lessons.excerpt: Switch the XML namespace on a single element to XHTML and the browser renders it as HTML directly inside the SVG.

lessons.point: Response headers can load stylesheets in Firefox, so a clean body is not enough.
lessons.excerpt: Firefox lets you load external CSS files using a Link response header.

lessons.point: An uploaded GIF can carry an SVG payload that Safari imports.
lessons.excerpt: if you can upload a GIF that contains the payload, it won't render when you open it in the browser, but it can still be imported with a `<use>` element!

entries.takeaway: If you accept SVG uploads, sanitize with DOMPurify or darylldoyle/svg-sanitizer, serve user files from a separate origin, and never let users influence response headers.

actionable.title: Audit which SVG sanitizer you use
actionable.detail: If your app uses mattkrick/sanitize-svg, Borewit/svg-sanitizer, bgalek/safe-svg, alnorris/SVG-Sanitizer, cloudflare/svg-hush or jams2/py-svg-hush, switch to DOMPurify or darylldoyle/svg-sanitizer. Serve uploaded images from a separate cookieless origin with a strict CSP, and make sure no user input reaches Link headers.

entries.verify_note: All claims supported; 'held' covers only these techniques and the GIF is SVG text under a .gif name. Novelty lowered to its 62.
entries.prior_art: SVG XSS and sanitizer bypasses are a long-running topic, and the post cites Kevin Mizu's animateTransform trick; the Link-header stylesheet execution in Firefox and Safari's GIF-as-SVG import are new.
entries.threat: Stored XSS through uploaded SVG or image files that pass a sanitizer.
entries.conditions: Applications that accept SVG or image uploads and serve them from the main origin using one of the six bypassed sanitizers.
entries.mitigations: Use DOMPurify or darylldoyle/svg-sanitizer, serve uploads from a separate origin with a strict CSP, and keep user input out of response headers.

entries.title: Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-88771 is a pre-auth command injection zero-day in default configuration
entries.summary: CVE-2026-88771 lets an unauthenticated attacker run commands as root on Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway in the default configuration, and it was exploited in the wild before a patch existed. The bug is in a crash-reporting Perl script (ns_monuploadd_err.pl) that reads appliance logs, pulls a core-file name out of them without validating it, and passes it to a shell command. Any request field that ends up in the logs, such as a login name or User-Agent header, can carry the attack, and the fix builds the name only from strictly matched fields and calls find without a shell.

lessons.point: The flaw affects the default configuration and was exploited as a zero-day before Citrix shipped a fix, so any unpatched internet-facing appliance should be treated as possibly compromised.
lessons.excerpt: It affects the default configuration and was exploited in the wild as a zero-day, before any fix existed.

lessons.point: Root cause: a log-parsing script trusts whatever text follows NSPPE in a log line as a core-file name and process ID, then interpolates it into a shell command.
lessons.excerpt: The problem is that the script never verifies that those first two fields are really an `nsppe` core file name and a numeric process ID.

lessons.point: The attack surface is any input that gets logged, not one endpoint, so blocking a single URL is not a complete mitigation; patching is required.
lessons.excerpt: Any endpoint or port that logs data controlled in an HTTP header can trigger this vulnerability.

lessons.point: The fix builds the value only from tightly matched captures. It runs external commands in list form, so no shell interprets metacharacters.
lessons.excerpt: Perl does not build a command string and does not start `/bin/sh`, so shell metacharacters cannot be interpreted as commands.

lessons.point: The same bulletin (CTX697096) has a sibling bug, CVE-2026-88778, that the upgrade alone does not fix; it needs a configuration change.
lessons.excerpt: Fixed by enabling Enhanced ISN Generation, not by the upgrade alone.

entries.takeaway: Patch NetScaler ADC and Gateway to 14.1-73.37 / 13.1-64.23 (or the FIPS/NDcPP equivalents) now, enable Enhanced ISN Generation, and hunt for compromise, because this root-level pre-auth bug was exploited before a fix existed.

actionable.title: Patch, harden and hunt on NetScaler ADC/Gateway for CVE-2026-88771 and siblings
actionable.detail: 1) Inventory all NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances, including management interfaces. 2) Upgrade to 14.1-73.37+, 13.1-64.23+, 14.1-73.37 FIPS+, or 13.1-37.279+ (13.1-FIPS/NDcPP) per Citrix bulletin CTX697096; if you cannot patch at once, take internet-facing appliances offline or restrict access, as watchTowr advised. 3) Enable Enhanced ISN Generation for CVE-2026-88778, which the upgrade alone does not fix. 4) Hunt: because exploitation went through logged fields, review appliance logs (AAA/SSLVPN login records, User-Agent and request-parameter entries) for usernames or headers containing 'pitboss' or 'NSPPE' text alongside shell metacharacters such as semicolons or backticks, and check for unexpected files in temp directories and unexpected processes running as root. 5) Because the bug was exploited before disclosure, treat unpatched exposed appliances as possibly compromised: rotate credentials and session secrets handled by the appliance and review downstream access from it.

entries.prior_art: Earlier NetScaler pre-auth bugs in the archive, e.g. 'Citrix NetScaler Pre-Auth Heap Overflow (CVE-2026-8452) ... SAML Signature Canonicalization' (memory corruption in nsppe); this one is a different class (shell injection via log content in a Perl helper script) outside nsppe. Verifier's closest: watchTowr Citrix NetScaler CVE-2026-8452; known appliance command-injection patches.
entries.verify_note: Verifier: versions, CVE-2026-88778, zero-day and default-configuration claims match; lessons 3-4 slightly over-generalize.
entries.threat: Unauthenticated remote attacker runs arbitrary commands as root on the NetScaler appliance, the front door for enterprise remote access; exploited in the wild as a zero-day alongside the DTLS memory overflow CVE-2026-88772.
entries.conditions: NetScaler ADC / NetScaler Gateway in default configuration on builds before the fixed versions (watchTowr diffed vulnerable 14.1 build 73.30 against fixed 73.37). Attacker-controlled text must reach appliance logs that ns_monuploadd_err.pl later parses, which login fields, headers and the management interface all allow.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to 14.1-73.37+, 13.1-64.23+, 14.1-73.37 FIPS+, or 13.1-37.279+ for 13.1-FIPS/NDcPP; enable Enhanced ISN Generation for CVE-2026-88778; take unpatched exposed appliances offline or restrict access; hunt logs for shell metacharacters in logged usernames and headers; assume compromise on appliances that were exposed and unpatched.

issues: mild: sentence_words 49 > 45 (4) Hunt: because exploitation went through logged fields, review appliance logs (AAA/SSLVPN login records, User-Agent an)
mild: acronyms 6 > 3 (ADC, FIPS, ISN, NSPPE, AAA, SSLVPN)

editorial.reason: Pre-auth root command injection in NetScaler ADC/Gateway exploited as a zero-day in default configuration; concrete fixed builds, a sibling bug the upgrade alone doesn't fix, and log-hunting guidance.

entries.title: Trail of Bits: only Go and vcpkg verified every downloaded package
entries.summary: Trail of Bits built a Docker and mitmproxy harness that played a compromised package repository and injected malware into real packages. Of 25 package managers, fewer than half verified lockfile hashes by default, and only Go and vcpkg verified every package they downloaded. Some lockfiles carry hashes that don't protect integrity: Pub warns on a mismatch but installs anyway, Conan's MD5 revision is an identifier, and CocoaPods and Composer hashes don't cover the fetched code.
entries.takeaway: A committed lockfile doesn't protect you from a compromised registry unless your package manager actually enforces its hashes; check yours and turn on the strict flag.

lessons.point: Integrity by default is rare: only two of 25 package managers verified every package they downloaded.
lessons.excerpt: fewer than half used lockfiles that checked for tampering by default, and only two verified the integrity of every package they downloaded

lessons.point: A hash in the lockfile is not enough: Pub detects a mismatch, rewrites the lockfile and installs the tampered package unless you pass --enforce-lockfile.
lessons.excerpt: If there is a mismatch, Pub detects the error, but installs the package anyway.

lessons.point: pnpm had the same overwrite-on-mismatch default until version 11.4 in May 2026.
lessons.excerpt: Overwriting the lockfile after a hash mismatch was also the default behavior in pnpm until version

lessons.point: Commit or tag hashes that don't cover the downloaded artifact give no protection: Composer pins a commit but downloads a ZIP that can't be checked against it.
lessons.excerpt: Once again, GitHub could serve a malicious ZIP archive without detection by Composer.

actionable.title: Enforce lockfile hashes in CI for every ecosystem you use
actionable.detail: Commit lockfiles for applications and install with the strict mode: npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile (pnpm 11.4 or later), yarn --immutable, flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile, uv/Poetry lock installs, and pip with hashes (pip --require-hashes). For NuGet set RestorePackagesWithLockFile. Treat Maven, Composer, CocoaPods, Conan, Gem and cpanminus as having no repository-compromise protection, and mirror or vendor their dependencies. Move cpanminus off plain HTTP.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: every fact checks out (source text truncated before the signature section; Table 2 supports the Go claim). Verifier novelty 50, relevance 72; took the lower novelty.
entries.prior_art: Prior work covers maintainer compromise and install-time code execution (pool claim package-installers-run-arbitrary-code-by-default) and the Gamage et al. lockfile study; this is the first cross-ecosystem dynamic test of 25 managers against a malicious repository, with per-manager verdicts.
entries.threat: An attacker who compromises a package repository or its web front end can serve modified packages that most package managers install without detecting tampering.
entries.conditions: Package managers that lack lockfile hashes, don't verify them by default, or whose hashes don't cover the downloaded artifact; cpanminus additionally fetches over plain HTTP.
entries.mitigations: Commit lockfiles and install in strict or frozen mode, enable signature verification where supported, mirror or vendor dependencies for ecosystems without integrity checks, and switch cpanminus to HTTPS mirrors.

editorial.reason: First cross-ecosystem test of package managers against a malicious registry; tells teams exactly which strict lockfile flags to turn on.

entries.title: Microsoft says Storm-0940 used the ARTEX pentest framework against 2,250+ tenants
entries.summary: Microsoft says Storm-0940 used ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent penetration-testing framework, to run password spraying, reconnaissance and OAuth-application abuse at machine speed after the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise. The actor tried to sign in to more than 2,250 tenants, and in several cases went from first targeting to privileged cloud access in under 3 hours. Most attempts failed, but the speed left defenders little time to respond.

lessons.point: Agentic tooling is already used by a state-aligned actor to scale known tradecraft such as spraying and OAuth abuse.
lessons.excerpt: ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing framework that can use any AI model to automate a variety of offensive security workflows.

lessons.point: Time to privileged cloud access fell under 3 hours in several cases.
lessons.excerpt: Several of these Storm-0940 ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the actor obtaining privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure – including multiple instances where the time from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours.

lessons.point: Alerts fire, but the pace outruns coordinated response.
lessons.excerpt: the speed of the activity allows very little time for Defenders to respond to those alerts and remediate the actor’s access in a coordinated fashion.

lessons.point: Hunt for service-principal sign-ins and unexpected credential or privilege changes on applications.
lessons.excerpt: Customers should review service principal sign-ins, investigate unexpected application credential or privilege changes

entries.takeaway: Agent-driven intrusions compress the time from first touch to privileged cloud access to hours, so detection and OAuth-app hygiene must work at machine speed.

actionable.title: Audit OAuth apps and service principals
actionable.detail: List enterprise apps and service principals with tenant-wide consent, review recent credential additions and privilege changes through Microsoft Graph, and alert on bursts of sign-in failures per minute. Rehearse a response that assumes hours, not days.

entries.prior_art: Earlier pool entries cover AI-orchestrated attacks compressing human timelines (claim agent-orchestrated-attacks-compress-human-attack-timelines); this adds a named state actor, a named framework and measured tenant scale. Verifier: Anthropic GTG-1002 (Nov 2025) AI-orchestrated espionage report; Google GTIG AI misuse reports. Delta is a named open-source agentic pentest framework (ARTEX) us
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every claim supported by the source.

editorial.reason: Microsoft attributes machine-speed ConnectWise supply-chain follow-on attacks to an agentic pentest framework.

entries.title: With ChatGPT, ITRES rebuilt two BruCON techniques whose source was never released
entries.summary: A researcher with no recent kernel experience used ChatGPT, conference slide photos, Git history and a compiled executable to rebuild two Windows kernel execution-redirection techniques shown at BruCON 2026. The original author had spent about four months on them and never released source. Both techniques reached SYSTEM on Windows 11 with VBS (virtualization-based security), HVCI (hypervisor-protected code integrity) and kernel shadow stacks enabled, after about 24 hours of recorded work. The model refused 39 times and broke working code late in the project, so the last integration step was finished by hand.

lessons.point: Partial public material (slides, Git history, a compiled binary) was enough to reconstruct unreleased techniques with LLM help.
lessons.excerpt: Using public research, Git history and a compiled executable, we went on to reconstruct and reproduce two of his techniques: Native SSDT and Shadow SSDT.

lessons.point: The author argues researchers should rethink how hard it is for others to weaponize partial disclosures.
lessons.excerpt: But the assumptions about how difficult it is for someone else to turn partial published information into custom working code may no longer be valid.

lessons.point: Model refusals were frequent but inconsistent: it helped build similar functionality earlier, then refused the final integration.
lessons.excerpt: That is approximately 13.8% of the 282 final assistant responses.

lessons.point: Offline test harnesses validated parsing logic only; real kernel effects needed a protected Windows lab with A/B/A restore checks.
lessons.excerpt: They didn’t prove that we could modify kernel execution, restore the original state or obtain a SYSTEM identity.

entries.takeaway: The author argues LLMs make partially disclosed exploit research much cheaper to reproduce, so release decisions for talks, binaries and repos should assume others can rebuild it.

actionable.title: Treat released binaries and slides as reproducible source
actionable.detail: Before publishing exploit research, assume a compiled PoC, slide photos and Git history can be turned into working code by an LLM-assisted non-expert within days. Scrub binaries and history you do not intend to release (deleting a repo late does not undo earlier clones), and plan defender guidance (detections, patches) to land with the talk, not after.

entries.prior_art: Closest pool work covers frontier AI agents compressing intrusion timelines (archive: 'Frontier AI Agents Compress a Two-Week Intrusion Into 10 Hours') and LLM research harnesses finding bugs (PwnEscape); this adds a measured case of LLM-assisted reproduction of unreleased kernel exploitation research from partial artifacts, plus refusal counts. Verifier: Earlier work showed LLMs speeding up exploit reproduction from partial information (e.g., GPT-4 one-day exploitation from CVE descriptions, Fang et al. 2024; AI-assisted n-day patch-diff reproduction). This adds a concrete kernel/HVCI case study with refusal counts, but the thesis itself is not new.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: Attackers with modest expertise can rebuild unreleased exploitation techniques from conference talks, deleted repos and compiled PoCs using general-purpose LLMs.
entries.conditions: Partial technical material is public (slides, Git history, a compiled executable); the reproduced techniques still require administrator privileges to load or use the tooling.
entries.mitigations: Researchers: avoid publishing compiled PoCs or history you do not intend to release; coordinate defensive guidance with disclosure. Defenders: keep VBS/HVCI enabled and monitor for vulnerable driver loading and admin-to-kernel paths.

editorial.reason: tl;dr sec-featured case of an LLM-assisted researcher rebuilding Windows kernel techniques from slides and a binary in about 24 hours; it changes how to weigh partial disclosure.

entries.title: @subql/common@5.8.3 npm package carried a backdoor that runs on install
entries.summary: On 5 October 2026 the maintainer account ianhe8x twice created and deleted a temporary branch in subquery/subql; the first run was a 'Red Team Canary (harmless)' workflow that published 5.8.3-onf-rt1 to test the path. The second was a release commit that, after yarn build, downloads a tarball from ci-artifacts.dev and overwrites packages/common with no hash or signature check before publishing 5.8.3; neither commit landed on main. The payload is about 83 KB of JavaScript behind XOR+gzip, PBKDF2 string encryption and AES-GCM-wrapped objects. It starts in a detached child process from both postinstall and module import, collects credentials (including from CI runner memory), and supports a remote shell; the published source map shows a harmless skeleton. 19 of 77 @subql packages' latest versions could resolve to 5.8.3 through ~ or ^ ranges.
entries.takeaway: A publish pipeline that builds from source and then fetches an external artifact is not building from source, and ignore-scripts does not help when the payload also fires on import.

lessons.point: Import-time triggers make install-script blocking insufficient on its own.
lessons.excerpt: Disabling install scripts alone is insufficient because importing the package also starts the payload.

lessons.point: The tampering sat between build and publish: the workflow discarded the built output and shipped an unverified external tarball.
lessons.excerpt: The new step then removes `packages/common` and replaces it with files downloaded from `ci-artifacts.dev`.

lessons.point: Source maps can be decoys; review the published JavaScript, not the mapped TypeScript.
lessons.excerpt: Reviewing the mapped source alone would therefore miss the payload and automatic triggers visible in the published JavaScript.

lessons.point: Exact-pinning a top-level package does not pin its transitive ranges; lockfiles are what freeze a shared dependency.
lessons.excerpt: Pinning one of these parent packages to an exact version does not, by itself, pin its dependencies.

actionable.title: Alert on publishes from non-default branches and on network fetches between build and publish
actionable.detail: Treat @subql/common@5.8.3 as malicious: block it and ci-artifacts.dev, check lockfiles for it (including transitive via @subql/cli, node-core, query, node-ethereum and node-*), and rotate secrets on any host or CI runner that installed or imported it. For your own projects, require that publish workflows only run from the protected default branch (environment branch rules on the npm publish environment) and fail any workflow diff that adds curl/wget/tar steps after the build step. Also compare the published tarball against a rebuild from the tagged commit before promoting it to latest.

entries.verify_note: All facts and excerpts supported. Verifier: the lockfile point in lesson 4 is the analyst's inference. Verifier novelty 55.
entries.prior_art: Close to the same week's tensorlake compromise and the keyv/ChainDrop cases in the archive (maintainer-account abuse of a legitimate release workflow, import-time payloads defeating ignore-scripts). Differs in method: publishing from a throwaway branch that was created and deleted twice and never merged, a 'canary' dry run first, and post-build artifact substitution from an external host instead of committing the payload to source; plus a decoy source map.
entries.threat: Compromised or misused maintainer account modifies the release workflow on a temporary branch to publish an externally supplied backdoored build of a shared Web3 indexing library.
entries.conditions: Any project that installs or imports @subql/common@5.8.3, directly or via @subql parent packages whose ~5.8.x or ^5.8.x ranges resolve to it; targets developer workstations and CI runners including GitHub Actions.
entries.mitigations: Pin @subql/common to 5.8.2 in lockfiles; block ci-artifacts.dev; investigate and rotate credentials where 5.8.3 ran; restrict publish environments to protected branches and review workflow changes.

entries.title: Valid SQL crashes SQLGlot and SQLFluff with huge memory amplification
entries.summary: SQLGlot and SQLFluff parse deeply nested or very wide but syntactically valid SQL with no depth or node limit: about 50 nesting levels hits Python's recursion limit, and a sub-2MB query builds an abstract syntax tree (AST) using over 1.5GB of RAM. Because apps parse before executing, one authenticated Superset SQL Lab user can kill or pin the shared worker pool, a Dify plugin query broke the daemon-to-worker bridge for about 60 seconds, and Pathway was OOM-killed at 8GB+. The same flaw shows up in Neo4j Cypher, graphql-js and graphql-core.
entries.takeaway: Treat any parser that consumes user or LLM-generated text as a trust boundary: cap bytes, depth and node count before parsing, and upgrade SQLGlot/SQLFluff to versions with limits.

lessons.point: Recursive-descent parsers without a depth cap fail on modest nesting.
lessons.excerpt: At 50+ levels of nesting, the recursive descent parser exhausts the call stack.

lessons.point: The DoS fires in the pre-execution parse step, so database-side limits and query timeouts don't help.
lessons.excerpt: An authenticated user with ordinary SQL Lab access is enough; the query never has to run.

lessons.point: Client-side input limits are not a control; enforce size caps on the server.
lessons.excerpt: The frontend enforces a 3,000-character input limit. The backend does not.

lessons.point: The bug class is generic to parsers that build rich object trees, not specific to SQL.
lessons.excerpt: Any parser that turns untrusted text into a rich object tree without bounding depth or node count is exposed.

actionable.title: Bound parser input before parsing
actionable.detail: Upgrade SQLGlot (limit merged ahead of v30.5.0) and SQLFluff to patched releases and keep default limits on. Where a parser takes user or LLM-generated SQL/GraphQL/Cypher, reject on cheap pre-parse checks on the server (byte size, token count, parenthesis depth, column count), run parsing with a timeout in a memory-capped worker or subprocess, and rate-limit submissions. For graphql-js and graphql-core, set an explicit max token/depth limit since none is on by default.

entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim. Verifier: the two CVEs were assigned to the SQLFluff findings only, and ~750x was measured on SQLGlot. Verifier novelty 55.
entries.prior_art: Classic algorithmic-complexity and deep-nesting DoS (billion laughs, JSON/YAML nesting bombs, GraphQL depth/complexity limits, Imperva's own graphql-java DoS write-up). New here: CVEs in the two main Python SQL parsers, measured amplification ratios, and concrete cascades into Superset, Dify and Pathway.
entries.threat: An authenticated low-privilege user (or anyone reaching an exposed parse endpoint) sends a valid but deeply nested or very wide query that exhausts memory or CPU in the parser, crashing or hanging shared workers.
entries.conditions: Application passes untrusted or LLM-generated SQL to unpatched SQLGlot or SQLFluff (or graphql-js/graphql-core/Cypher without limits) with no server-side size or depth cap.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade parsers and keep recursion/node limits enabled; server-side byte/token/depth/column caps before parsing; parse timeouts; container memory limits; rate limiting; isolate plugin processes.

entries.title: Unit 42: ransomware groups try PAN-OS CVE-2026-0257 to bypass GlobalProtect MFA
entries.summary: Unit 42 updated its report on CVE-2026-0257, a GlobalProtect authentication bypass fixed in May 2026. Unit 42 saw exploitation attempts by ransomware operators including Qilin and Inc against unpatched devices; successful ones open VPN sessions that skip MFA, followed by RMM tools, RDP and SMB. In one notable case the attackers pivoted to vCenter and ESXi and dumped domain-controller credentials offline from the virtual disk, bypassing in-guest EDR.

lessons.point: Exploitation yields an MFA-free VPN foothold.
lessons.excerpt: Attackers are leveraging this vulnerability to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, subsequently bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session.

lessons.point: The key change is going to the virtualization layer.
lessons.excerpt: The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer.

lessons.point: Offline credential theft sidesteps in-guest detection.
lessons.excerpt: This tactic bypasses in-guest endpoint detection and response (EDR) and security controls

lessons.point: A fix has existed for months.
lessons.excerpt: Fixes for this vulnerability have been available since May 2026.

entries.takeaway: Patch GlobalProtect and protect the hypervisor management plane: in one case attackers read virtual disks to go around endpoint tools.

actionable.title: Close the hypervisor blind spot
actionable.detail: Patch PAN-OS or apply the mitigations (dedicated Authentication Override certificate or disable the option), isolate vCenter and ESXi management, and alert on execInstalledOnly changes and VMDK reads outside backup tools.

entries.prior_art: Ransomware targeting ESXi is established; the offline VMDK credential-dumping pivot after a VPN bypass is the new detail. Verifier: Hypervisor-targeting ransomware (ESXi encryptors, Scattered Spider vCenter/ESXi pivots, Mandiant UNC3944 reports); offline NTDS extraction from VMDK is document

entries.title: Citizen Lab: Candiru spyware reached Al Jazeera devices through targeted ads
entries.summary: Citizen Lab reports AdFection: Candiru spyware infected Al Jazeera devices through targeted advertisements, which it calls the first public technical confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through ads. Discover-Tech, an Israeli firm that looks like a normal ad company, ran a platform that fingerprints devices and infects them when an ad renders. Four billion bidding records show its ads on almost 200,000 sites and apps. Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi cut its access after disclosure.

lessons.point: Ads delivered a zero-click mercenary spyware attack.
lessons.excerpt: first public technical confirmation of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack delivered via targeted advertising, which we call AdFection

lessons.point: Ad industry vendor lists failed to catch the abuse.
lessons.excerpt: Discover-Tech has appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe

lessons.point: Scale: ads reached nearly 200,000 sites and apps in four months.
lessons.excerpt: Analysis of four billion Discover-Tech bidding records shows that during a four-month period, the company’s ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries.

lessons.point: Disconnecting the vendor was possible after disclosure.

actionable.detail: For journalists and executives, enable lockdown or hardened modes, use a content blocker or DNS filtering for ad networks, and keep mobile OS updates current; add ad-exchange vendor review to threat models.

entries.title: EDK2 network boot flaw lets attackers run code before Secure Boot
entries.summary: CVE-2026-97631 (severity 9.5) is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the network boot (PXE) driver of TianoCore EDK2. EDK2 is the open source base most UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) firmware is built on. During network boot, an oversized ICMP error message overflows a 504-byte field, which can let an attacker run code at the highest CPU privilege before Secure Boot and TPM (Trusted Platform Module) protections apply. The planned coordinated disclosure broke early when a vendor's public pull request published the fix, and the article says an attacker needs some control over a local network and an exploit tuned to each target.

lessons.point: The bug is a bounds error in copying ICMP error messages during PXE boot.
lessons.excerpt: for a message longer than 504 bytes it still copies bytes into the field

lessons.point: Fuzzing campaigns started after the similar PixieFail bug did not find this flaw.
lessons.excerpt: It appears those efforts failed to find this latest flaw.

lessons.point: Exploits must be tuned to each firmware build, which limits mass exploitation.
lessons.excerpt: but it needs to be tuned for each target model/version/configuration since the addresses will change based on those

lessons.point: Turning off network boot is the main interim mitigation, since Secure Boot and TPM do not stop this bug.
lessons.excerpt: they should consider turning off network boot capabilities at least temporarily if possible

entries.takeaway: Any server fleet that network-boots on EDK2-based firmware has a pre-OS code-execution hole, so disable PXE where you can and push your firmware vendors for updates.

actionable.title: Inventory PXE-booting EDK2 machines and disable network boot
actionable.detail: Identify servers and storage that boot from the local network on EDK2-derived firmware (AMI, Insyde, Phoenix, Project Mu). Disable PXE where it is not needed, ask each firmware vendor for a fixed BIOS/UEFI update for CVE-2026-97631, and watch for oversized ICMP error traffic on boot network segments.

entries.prior_art: No UEFI, EDK2 or PXE entries in the pools. The source names PixieFail, an earlier EDK2 PXE flaw class, as the closest precedent.
entries.threat: An attacker on the local network sends an oversized ICMP error during PXE boot and overflows the driver buffer. This gives ring-0 code execution before Secure Boot and TPM protections, which could defeat disk encryption, or simply hangs the boot.
entries.conditions: Machines whose firmware is built on EDK2 with PXE network boot enabled (on by default) and that boot from the network, with the attacker on the network and knowing the target firmware build. Machines that boot only from disk are not affected.
entries.mitigations: Apply the BIOS/UEFI update from your firmware vendor, temporarily disable network boot where possible, keep TPM and Secure Boot enabled, and monitor logs for exploitation attempts.

entries.title: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs carry a security smell
entries.author: A H M Nazmus Sakib et al.
entries.summary: A large-scale study of the AIDev dataset classified security smells across 16,112 file changes in 4,022 agent-generated pull requests. 38.9% of agent PRs contain at least one security smell and supply-chain integrity issues make up 82.3% of them - but the counterintuitive result is that human collaborators introduce 67.6% of the genuine leaked secrets in these agent-assisted workflows, and review catches almost none of them. All percentages are downstream of an LLM-as-a-judge classification pipeline plus manual review, so treat the precision of the figures accordingly.

lessons.point: Supply-chain integrity dominates the detected smell taxonomy (82.3%); the abstract does not enumerate the remaining categories, so everything else combined is a small residual - point provenance and dependency controls at agent output.
lessons.excerpt: 38.9% of agent-generated PRs contain at least one security smell, with supply chain integrity issues accounting for 82.3% of all detected security smells

lessons.point: Blaming the agent misreads the data: humans introduced most genuine leaked secrets, which the authors describe only as suggesting a *potential* reduction in developer vigilance - an association, not a causal finding.
lessons.excerpt: human collaborators are responsible for introducing 67.6% of genuine leaked secrets within these agent-assisted workflows

lessons.point: Existing review is not a control here - automated and human review together missed 81.1% of these credentials before integration.
lessons.excerpt: existing automated and human review processes fail to detect 81.1% of these credentials prior to integration

entries.threat: Security debt accumulates in high-impact file paths faster than human review capacity, with hard-coded credentials making up 99.6% of critical-severity smells.
entries.conditions: Repositories that accept autonomous coding-agent pull requests through a conventional human review process.
entries.mitigations: Enforce secret scanning as a merge gate rather than a review step; apply provenance/dependency-integrity checks to agent PRs; add context-aware guardrails at the human-AI collaboration point rather than at final review.
entries.takeaway: Gate agent PRs with automated secret and dependency-integrity checks - human review demonstrably does not catch this class, and the humans are introducing most of it.
entries.prior_art: That LLM-generated code contains vulnerabilities is well documented (Copilot-era studies onward). The delta is scale and attribution on real agent PRs - the 67.6% human-origin secrets finding inverts the 'the agent is the risk' framing. Methodologically it applies an existing technique (LLM-as-judge + manual coding) to a new dataset rather than introducing a new method. Accepted at the KDD 2026 AgenticSE workshop.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: removed invented contrast categories (injection/logic bugs); restored the authors' 'potential' hedge on developer vigilance; surfaced that all figures come from an LLM-as-a-judge pipeline; novelty 68->57.

editorial.reason: Large-scale, widely-discussed finding on coding-agent risk with a concrete gate: automated secret + dependency-integrity scanning on agent PRs, because human review misses 81%.

entries.title: Alpine Linux rebuilt GitLab after its upgrade missed a Ruby patch
entries.summary: On October 20 and 21 a newly registered account sent crafted CI configurations to Alpine Linux's GitLab to exploit CVE-2026-97229, a CVSS 10.0 bug in Ruby's Onigmo regular expression engine, crashing workers 8 times. Alpine's upgrade to GitLab 19.3.6 did not fix it, because the fix is a patch GitLab applies to Ruby only in its official packages and Alpine's image used stock Ruby; self-built installs also need Ruby 3.3.13, 3.4.12 or 4.0.9. Alpine found no evidence of code execution but could not rule it out, so it rebuilt the instance, reset all passwords and secret keys, and verified packages and releases against records outside GitLab.

lessons.point: A vendor's fix can live in a patched runtime it bundles, so upgrading the application alone leaves source or self-built installs vulnerable.
lessons.excerpt: The fix isn’t in GitLab’s own code but in a patch to Ruby, which GitLab applies only in its official packages.

lessons.point: The attacker pulled Alpine's public container image, likely to tune the exploit to the exact build, so publishing your images helps attackers fit exploits to you.
lessons.excerpt: The attacker also downloaded our GitLab container image, which suggests they were tuning the exploit to our exact build.

lessons.point: Without outbound connection logs, Alpine could not prove the exploit failed, which forced a full rebuild.
lessons.excerpt: We had no logging of outbound network connections, and our hosting provider keeps none either.

lessons.point: Keeping signing keys off the forge and checking commits against independent records let Alpine clear its packages and releases despite the uncertainty.
lessons.excerpt: The keys that sign Alpine packages and releases are not, and never have been, stored on the GitLab server.

entries.takeaway: If you build GitLab yourself, check what runtime patches its official packages carry, and log outbound traffic so you can rule a compromise in or out.

actionable.title: Check bundled-runtime patches when you self-build vendor software
actionable.detail: For self-managed GitLab built from source or on your own image, confirm Ruby is 3.3.13, 3.4.12, 4.0.9 or later, not just the GitLab version. For each critical release, read whether the fix sits in a bundled component your build must apply. Record outbound connections from the host, keep logs longer than 14 days, and keep signing keys off the forge.

entries.verify_note: Verifier upheld all four lessons (novelty 55 vs 50, lower kept).
entries.prior_art: The pool has GitLab's advisory for a different CVSS 10.0 regex RCE (CVE-2026-110264, 19.5.1 patch release), which is a vendor patch notice. This entry adds a first-hand incident: the fix lived in a bundled Ruby patch that self-built installs missed, plus the forensic limits that forced a rebuild.
entries.threat: An attacker with a self-registered account submits crafted CI configurations that trigger an Onigmo regex engine bug for possible code execution on the GitLab server, exposing user data, password hashes, two-factor authentication secrets, CI/CD variables, runner tokens and private repositories.
entries.conditions: Self-managed GitLab without the October 12 fix, or GitLab built on standard Ruby older than 3.3.13, 3.4.12 or 4.0.9, with open account registration.
entries.mitigations: Use GitLab's official packages or upgrade Ruby to a fixed release, apply critical GitLab releases within a day, log outbound and database connections and keep logs longer, keep signing keys off the forge, and sign release tags so releases can be verified outside GitLab.
entries.author: sashk

editorial.reason: First-hand incident on a CVSS 10.0 GitLab bug: the fix lived in a bundled Ruby patch that self-built installs miss, and missing egress logs forced a full rebuild.

entries.title: CrowdStrike: four newly seen actors ran agentic Claude Code intrusions
entries.summary: CrowdStrike analyzed four previously unreported actors (not all clearly criminal) that left offensive agent frameworks exposed (May to August 2026). One built a Supervisor and Executor pair of Claude Code agents derived from PentestGPT and hit at least 15 healthcare entities; one used two harnesses and a China-based API proxy; one used 819 skills from GitHub and had to coax the model past guardrails; one used a single slash command with a seven-step workflow. CrowdStrike judges that agentic AI commoditizes baseline offensive operations.

lessons.point: Agentic AI lowers the cost of baseline offensive operations.
lessons.excerpt: The four cases documented in this report likely demonstrate that agentic AI commoditizes baseline offensive cyber operations.

lessons.point: A supervisor/executor split with a state machine structures the attack.
lessons.excerpt: a “Supervisor” Claude Code agent selects the next task from a state machine (i.e., a predefined workflow of attack stages) and an “Executor” agent performs the task.

lessons.point: Guardrails slowed but did not stop the weakest actor, who nudged the model.
lessons.excerpt: the threat actor periodically had to intervene to overcome the model’s safety guardrails or to exhort Claude Code to keep trying to overcome a particular barrier.

lessons.point: CrowdStrike forecasts that low-skill actors will reach a higher capability level.
lessons.excerpt: Agentic AI will reduce barriers to effective intrusions

entries.takeaway: CrowdStrike expects low-skill actors to reach organized-crime-level effectiveness within 12 months, so harden against basic tradecraft now.

actionable.title: Plan for agent-speed basic attacks
actionable.detail: Close commodity paths (exposed services, weak creds, unpatched edge) and tune detections for rapid, systematic enumeration; add endpoint telemetry for coding-agent CLIs run by non-developers.
