entries.title: JFrog Artifactory auth bypass chain exploited in the wild leaves persistent backdoors
entries.summary: Wiz Research saw attackers chain two Artifactory flaws: an exposed anonymous-user token and a token-scope validation bug. They separately abused a critical default-config auth bypass to get admin control. After entry, attackers created admin accounts, deployed Groovy plugins for code execution, and stole Access signing keys. Upgrading therefore does not remove them. Some implants even live only in memory, hide from 2xx-based detection, and wipe logs.

lessons.point: Two individually non-admin bugs combined into an unauthenticated-to-admin path in two requests.
lessons.excerpt: Together, the two can turn an unauthenticated request into an admin-scoped token in two steps.

lessons.point: Patching closes the entry point but not persistence: plugins reload on restart and look like normal API traffic.
lessons.excerpt: are reloaded automatically on restart, and are reachable over ordinary, TLS-wrapped API traffic that is indistinguishable at the network layer from normal registry usage.

lessons.point: Stolen token-signing private keys let attackers mint valid tokens forever, so the token certificate must be reset, not just the software upgraded.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker holding `private.key` can therefore forge valid tokens for any user and any scope, indefinitely, without ever touching the compromised host again

lessons.point: Detections keyed to successful responses miss implants that return output through error responses.
lessons.excerpt: Detection logic that looks for successful (2xx) plugin executions will miss this backdoor entirely.

entries.takeaway: For an exposed artifact registry, patching is not remediation: hunt for rogue admins and plugins and rotate token-signing keys and every stored credential.

actionable.title: Post-exploitation hunt checklist for Artifactory
actionable.detail: If an instance was exposed while vulnerable, assume compromise. Review admin users (including accounts with names like jfrog-insight or repo-service), list Groovy files under the plugins directory, check for requests by token:anonymous to /access/api/v1/tokens and /api/plugins/execute/, look for HTTP 500 responses on plugin endpoints and truncated request logs, reset the Access token certificate and rotate LDAP, proxy and remote-repository credentials.

entries.prior_art: No Artifactory entries found in pool; the nearest are other KEV exploited-appliance entries, which lack this post-exploitation detail (patch-surviving plugins, in-memory servlet filter, key theft). Verifier: No Artifactory entry; nearest is the CISA KEV exploited-appliance entries and 'Wiz scans every new npm version at publish time...'; patch-surviving plugin backdoor plus signing-key theft is a new detail within the known 'patching is not remediation' pattern
entries.threat: Attackers chain Artifactory auth flaws (CVE-2026-42018 anonymous token exposure, CVE-2026-42016 scope validation, CVE-2026-82329 default-config admin bypass) to gain admin, then plant Groovy plugin backdoors, a Rust backdoor, an in-memory servlet filter, and steal Access signing keys and stored upstream credentials.
entries.conditions: Self-hosted Artifactory instances reachable over the network while running vulnerable versions; Wiz reports roughly two thirds of customers running Artifactory had a vulnerable instance at publication of each CVE.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to fixed versions, hunt for rogue admin accounts and plugins, reset the token certificate and Access keys, rotate stored credentials, and add behavioral detections for low-privilege identities minting tokens or touching the plugins API.
entries.verify_note: All four excerpts are verbatim and claims (67/69% exposure, 2-step chain, in-memory filter, HTTP 500 output, log purge) are supported. Source text is truncated at the CVE-2026-82329 detection section.

issues: mild: sentence_words 52 > 45 (Review admin users (including accounts with names like jfrog-insight or repo-service), list Groovy files under the plugi)

editorial.reason: In-the-wild exploitation of a JFrog Artifactory auth-bypass chain leaving Groovy plugin backdoors; teaches what to hunt for on a core build-infrastructure system.

entries.title: Google PageBreak finds 500+ XSS bugs with near-zero false positives
entries.summary: PageBreak is Google Product Security's internal agent, mostly running on Gemini models, that hunts bugs in Google's own web apps. The agent only proposes a bug. Hand-written (not AI-written) validators then fire a real payload per bug class (XSS, SQL injection, path traversal, RCE, server-side request forgery) against a running environment, and only confirmed findings reach product teams. That produced 500+ XSS bugs at near-zero false positives, while apps built on Google's secure-by-design frameworks yielded just 2.

lessons.point: The agent only proposes a bug. A separate deterministic validator confirms it by actually running an exploit payload.
lessons.excerpt: When the agent identifies a potential flaw, it passes the hypothesis to a validator which then executes a real payload to confirm the exploit.

lessons.point: Testing against a running environment cuts false positives and keeps 'AI slop' away from product teams.
lessons.excerpt: This approach results in a near-zero false positive rate, ensuring that we avoid overloading product teams with unverified vulnerability reports.

lessons.point: Unverified findings are not thrown away. They seed later runs and show where validators are missing, but they never go to developers.
lessons.excerpt: Crucially, we do not send these unverified candidates to product teams, preserving their focus for high-confidence alerts.

lessons.point: Asking the agent to report which capability or access it lacked turns failed validations into a roadmap for the harness.
lessons.excerpt: We let the PageBreak agent report what capabilities or environment access it is missing in order to validate a report.

lessons.point: Secure-by-design web frameworks held up against the agent: only 2 XSS bugs across hundreds of apps built on them, both in internal or debug endpoints.
lessons.excerpt: As of September 4, 2026, the scanner identified only 2 XSS vulnerabilities across hundreds of web applications built on these frameworks and those were limited to internal applications or debug endpoints with hardening gaps.

entries.takeaway: Let the AI agent propose bugs, report only what a non-AI validator confirms by exploitation, and treat safe-by-default frameworks as the stronger defense.

actionable.title: Put a per-bug-class exploit validator between your AI scanner and your bug tracker
actionable.detail: For each bug class you hunt, write a deterministic validator that is not AI-written. XSS: load the URL in a headless renderer and detect execution of a unique JavaScript marker. SQL injection: check output or timing differences. Path traversal: plant a file in a world-readable location and read it back through the app. RCE: sleep delay, file write, or outbound DNS/HTTP callback. Server-side request forgery (SSRF): detect an internal request reaching a canary. File only the confirmed findings. Keep unconfirmed ones as seeds for later runs, and log the capability or access the agent says it lacked.

entries.prior_art: Chainguard Athena write-up ('Gate agent-found vulnerabilities on host-side replay', archive.json); the general generate-then-verify pattern used by AI pentest agents such as XBOW and Google Big Sleep. New here: production-scale numbers (500+ XSS) and the framework-hardening comparison. Verifier's closest: Chainguard Athena host-side replay gate; XBOW and Big Sleep generate-then-verify.
entries.verify_note: Verifier: excerpts verbatim; 'near-zero false positives' is Google's own unquantified claim.
entries.threat: Noisy, unverified LLM vulnerability reports overwhelm product teams. Real XSS and similar bugs remain in large first-party web estates.
entries.conditions: Needs running test environments, scanning infrastructure that can authenticate to the apps, and validators for each bug class. Google also relies on its mono-repo and traffic-to-code mapping (Security Signals), which most organizations do not have.
entries.mitigations: Use secure-by-design web frameworks. Gate AI findings on deterministic exploit validation. Run agents across many iterations with identical seeds to improve the odds of finding a working exploit path.

editorial.reason: Google's production-scale numbers for AI web testing gated by non-AI exploit validators (500+ XSS, near-zero false positives, only 2 on its high-assurance frameworks) teach how to make agent-found bugs trustworthy.

entries.title: Sentry's tunnelRoute skipped middleware for the whole tunnel path, not just rewrites
entries.summary: @sentry/nextjs's tunnelRoute option forwards browser events through a path on your own Next.js server and tells the SDK to skip middleware for them. The skip matched every path under the tunnel prefix, while the rewrite only served the exact tunnel path with the o and p parameters, so any app route that resolves under that prefix (a direct collision or a root dynamic segment like app/[locale]) ran without middleware. It is only an authorization bypass where middleware is the sole authz layer; fixed in 9.47.2, 10.75.2 and 11.0.0-rc.1.

lessons.point: The bug is a scope mismatch: an exemption (skip middleware) was matched more broadly than the thing it existed to protect (the rewrite).
lessons.excerpt: The middleware skip was wider than the rewrite.

lessons.point: Requests in the gap reach application routes with middleware never executed.
lessons.excerpt: Requests in that gap go to your application instead of Sentry, and your middleware never runs on them.

lessons.point: It is only exploitable when middleware is the sole authorization layer for the colliding routes; server-side session checks still hold.
lessons.excerpt: your middleware is the only place that enforces authorization for those routes

lessons.point: The durable fix is defense in depth: enforce authorization in the route, layout or data-access layer as well as middleware.
lessons.excerpt: Enforce authorization in the route, layout or data-access path as well as in middleware.

lessons.point: Only webpack builds are affected.
lessons.excerpt: Turbopack builds are not affected

entries.threat: Unauthenticated access to Next.js routes whose only authorization check lives in middleware, by requesting them under the Sentry tunnel prefix.
entries.conditions: tunnelRoute set; webpack build; an app route resolving under the tunnel path (including a root dynamic segment); middleware-only authorization.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade @sentry/nextjs to 9.47.2 / 10.75.2 / 11.0.0-rc.1; move tunnelRoute to a path no route can resolve under; build with Turbopack; enforce authz in routes or data access, not only middleware.
entries.takeaway: Any SDK or framework that exempts paths from middleware is a potential authz bypass: if middleware is your only authorization check, grep your dependencies for middleware skips.

actionable.title: Audit middleware exemptions and add route-level authz
actionable.detail: Upgrade @sentry/nextjs; then list every matcher/skip that bypasses Next.js middleware (Sentry tunnel, static assets, health checks) and confirm each protected route also checks the session server-side in its layout, route handler or data-access layer.

entries.prior_art: Next.js CVE-2025-29927 (x-middleware-subrequest middleware bypass) established that middleware-only authorization in Next.js is fragile; this is a new, SDK-introduced instance of the same class.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all excerpts verbatim; novelty 40 (same); stressed the route-collision precondition and that server-side session checks still protect routes.

editorial.reason: Critical GHSA in a ubiquitous Next.js SDK with a transferable lesson: middleware exemptions are authz bypasses wherever middleware is the only authorization check.

entries.title: NorForge found exposed Cairn AI-pentest panels used by criminals and red teams
entries.summary: NorForge found more than 20 open Cairn panels, a web front for a state-based multi-agent engine that works from an origin to a goal using a shared blackboard of facts and operator hints. Many were tied to malicious activity and showed targets, found weaknesses, secrets and whether the target was compromised. A number of apparently legitimate red-team operations were exposed too, which can put clients at risk. NorForge withheld panel addresses until takedown.

lessons.point: Open agent panels give an unusually detailed view of attacker workflow.
lessons.excerpt: More than 20 exposed Cairn panels were identified as likely associated with malicious activity, providing an unusually detailed view of how threat actors select targets, direct autonomous agents, exploit vulnerabilities, and establish persistent access to compromised systems.

lessons.point: Legitimate red teams are exposed the same way, which endangers client data.
lessons.excerpt: In addition, a considerable number of apparently legitimate red team operations were also exposed this way, potentially placing clients at risk.

lessons.point: Cairn organizes work as projects with a start point and an end goal.
lessons.excerpt: In Cairn, each separate task is considered a project.

lessons.point: Agents share findings through a blackboard that humans can also edit.
lessons.excerpt: The agent posts every fact onto a project-internal blackboard.

entries.takeaway: AI pentest harnesses leak the targets and secrets they hold; lock down their UIs, and treat open panels as both an attacker intel source and a client-data risk.

actionable.title: Secure your own offensive tooling
actionable.detail: Put any AI pentest or agent harness UI behind authentication and a VPN, never on the open internet, and scan your own ranges on Shodan/Censys for such panels. Defenders can search for open panels to learn about active targeting.

entries.prior_art: Earlier reporting (Gambit Security, September) noted AI harnesses on attacker servers; NorForge gives the first panel-level view. Verifier: Gambit Security September 2026 report on AI harnesses (Hermes, Strix, Cairn) on an attacker staging server; classic exposed C2 and open-directory research. Delt

entries.title: GitHub Security Lab found 24 Android vulnerabilities with its AI agent
entries.summary: GitHub Security Lab extended its open-source Taskflow Agent with Android-specific audit steps. One taskflow separates mobile from non-mobile entry points, and another checks a fixed list of vulnerability classes against each entry point. Together they found 24 vulnerabilities, including OsmAnd location tracking and a WebView account-takeover chain. The post is candid that LLMs over-report low-severity bugs, misjudge severity, and need PoC runs plus expert review.

lessons.point: Give the model a per-entry-point checklist of vulnerability classes so non-determinism doesn't skip the essential bug classes on less familiar platforms like Android.
lessons.excerpt: Since mobile application vulnerabilities are less widely known and LLMs are non-deterministic, we should ensure the LLM checks for certain essential vulnerabilities classes.

lessons.point: Run a strict checklist prompt several times alongside a broad open-ended prompt: the first catches the obvious bugs and the second finds the creative ones.
lessons.excerpt: By combining both prompts across multiple runs, we get the best of each

lessons.point: LLM auditors over-report low-impact or unrealistic-state bugs, even when told not to, so every finding needs expert triage.
lessons.excerpt: it often reported low-severity vulnerabilities, even when specifically told not to do so

lessons.point: Making the model write a proof of concept surfaces mitigating factors it otherwise misses; a debugger is the stronger fix for the false positives that remain.
lessons.excerpt: the only way to fix these issue is to give the LLM a debugger to run the proof of concept and original code

entries.takeaway: Scaffolded, platform-specific taskflows make LLMs effective Android bug hunters, but severity and exploitability still need a PoC and a human.

actionable.title: Two-stage Android audit: classify entry points, then checklist per entry point
actionable.detail: Stage 1: enumerate exported activities, services, receivers, deeplinks and JS bridges, and separate mobile from non-mobile entry points. Stage 2: for each entry point, prompt for its class-specific checklist (intents: confused deputy, insecure broadcast; WebView: XSS, exposed bridges; files: path traversal). Run that strict pass several times plus one open-ended pass, then require a PoC for every finding before human triage.

entries.prior_art: Earlier GHSL Taskflow Agent posts on generic audit taskflows, and LLM-assisted SAST triage; the delta is the Android-specific entry-point and checklist decomposition plus its field results.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all lessons supported; novelty 45 (vs 50), relevance 80.

editorial.reason: 24 real, disclosed Android vulnerabilities (OsmAnd location tracking, a WebView account-takeover chain) found with an open-source agent you can run today, plus candid lessons on LLM severity misjudgment and false positives.

entries.title: tensorlake@0.5.144 npm worm spread from a hijacked admin account
entries.summary: On 7 October 2026 an attacker using a tensorlake repository admin account committed a Mini Shai-Hulud payload to main through the GitHub web UI (so every commit showed as 'verified'), then started the release workflow by hand. Version 0.5.144 (about 106,000 monthly downloads) shipped through npm trusted publishing with valid provenance and no stolen npm token. Its preinstall loader skips CI, downloads Bun, and runs an 856 KB worm. The worm steals cloud, GitHub, npm, SSH, browser and wallet credentials and republishes the victim's npm packages. It plants Claude Code and VS Code hooks, resolves its command-and-control (C2) server through an Ethereum contract, and installs a gh-token-monitor service that runs rm -rf ~/ when the stolen GitHub token stops working.
entries.takeaway: Provenance attestations and 'verified' commit badges prove where a build came from, not that the source is clean; and in this worm family, revoking the stolen GitHub token before removing gh-token-monitor wipes the victim's home directory.

lessons.point: No registry credential was needed: control of a repo admin account plus the project's own release workflow was enough to publish.
lessons.excerpt: The attacker did not need an npm token. They used a repository administrator account to commit the payload to `main` through the GitHub web interface.

lessons.point: Trusted publishing and SLSA provenance faithfully attest a poisoned build; they do not indicate the source is safe.
lessons.excerpt: The provenance is valid for a build of poisoned source.

lessons.point: Commits made in the GitHub web UI are signed by GitHub, so the 'verified' badge gives no signal about account compromise.
lessons.excerpt: GitHub signs web interface commits, so all eight show as verified.

lessons.point: Incident response order matters: the dead-man switch fires on revocation, so remove the monitor service first, then rotate tokens.
lessons.excerpt: If GitHub returns 40x, for example after revocation, it deletes the home directory.

actionable.title: Remove gh-token-monitor before revoking tokens, and gate release workflows on reviewed commits
actionable.detail: On any machine that installed tensorlake@0.5.144 (or another Mini Shai-Hulud package), first disable and delete gh-token-monitor (systemd user service, macOS LaunchAgent com.user.gh-token-monitor, or Windows scheduled task; files under ~/.config/gh-token-monitor/ and ~/.local/bin/gh-token-monitor.sh), then rotate GitHub, npm, cloud, SSH, AI-tool and browser-saved credentials. Hunt for public repos described 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again', commits authored as claude, and unexpected .claude/settings.json or .vscode/tasks.json. For your own packages: require PRs and reviews on the branch your publish workflow builds from, require a second approver (GitHub environment protection) for manually dispatched releases, and alert on direct pushes to main by admins. Block iseekaigogo.com and Ethereum RPC egress from developer machines where feasible.

entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim. Verifier: the token-revocation wiper arms only on some machines (accounts with no organizations, 24-hour watch), and the workflow was started on 8 Oct 00:08 UTC. Novelty lowered to the verifier's 40.
entries.prior_art: Same worm family as the keyv/cacheable Mini Shai-Hulud compromise and ChainDrop already in the archive (valid provenance, Bun loader, Ethereum-resolved C2, Claude Code/VS Code hooks). New here: delivery through an admin account's web-UI commits and a manually started trusted-publishing run instead of a stolen npm token, a new C2 domain and Ethereum contract, a browser password stealer, eval of C2 responses, and an identified rm -rf ~/ handler that arms only for tokens whose account has no organizations.
entries.threat: Compromised maintainer/admin GitHub account publishes a credential-stealing, self-propagating npm worm through the project's legitimate release pipeline.
entries.conditions: Developer workstation (loader exits on CI) runs npm install of tensorlake@0.5.144 with install scripts enabled; the destructive watcher arms when a stolen GitHub token belongs to an account with no organizations.
entries.mitigations: Pin tensorlake to 0.5.143 or upgrade to the reverted 0.5.145; set ignore-scripts for installs; remove gh-token-monitor before rotating credentials; enforce branch protection and release approvals so an admin account alone cannot ship from main.

editorial.reason: Live npm worm (two independent write-ups, SafeDep and StepSecurity) that published through the project's own trusted-publishing workflow and arms a home-directory wiper on token revocation: a concrete lesson that valid provenance doesn't…

entries.title: Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day used by ShinyHunters was three chained flaws
entries.summary: The PeopleSoft bug that ShinyHunters has exploited since May, patched as CVE-2026-35273 (CVSS 9.8), is really three flaws chained together. A server-side request forgery (the server can be made to send requests for the attacker) in the Integration Gateway reaches the internal Environment Management Hub. That hub trusts 127.0.0.1 by default, and from there an attacker can write a web shell or plant a malicious XML file, giving remote code execution with no login. Attackers got past web application firewall rules by URL-encoding one character of the blocked path.

lessons.point: A default allowlist entry for the loopback address turns any server-side request forgery into full access to internal admin interfaces.
lessons.excerpt: That file ships with the local loopback address, 127.0.0.1, already on the list.

lessons.point: Path-matching web application firewall rules can be bypassed by URL-encoding a single character, because the server decodes the path before serving it.
lessons.excerpt: Many WAF rules match the path's plain text, while the PeopleSoft server decodes it and serves the page.

lessons.point: The XMLDecoder code-execution path leaves no web shell behind, so web-shell hunting alone can miss it.
lessons.excerpt: The second path leaves less for standard detection to catch.

lessons.point: Patching does not remove an attacker who is already inside. Hunt for web shells and rotate credentials as well.
lessons.excerpt: Patching closes the door; it does not by itself evict someone already inside.

entries.takeaway: Treating loopback as trusted makes any request-forgery bug a way past the perimeter, so patch rather than relying on path-based firewall rules.

actionable.title: Patch PeopleSoft CVE-2026-35273 and remove PSEMHUB exposure
actionable.detail: Apply Oracle's security alert fix on PeopleTools 8.61/8.62. If you cannot patch yet, disable the Environment Management Hub (multi-server) or remove the PSEMHUB application (single-server). Do not rely on WAF rules that block /PSEMHUB/, since /%50SEMHUB/ gets past them. On hosts that may be compromised, hunt for web shells and unexpected XML files read at service start, and rotate every credential reachable from the PeopleSoft tier.

entries.prior_art: No PeopleSoft or ShinyHunters entries in the pools. Closest: the ai-security entry on loopback MCP servers needing Host/Origin checks, the same loopback-trust failure in a different product.
entries.threat: An unauthenticated attacker chains a server-side request forgery in PSIGW to the PSEMHUB admin interface, which trusts loopback, then gets code execution through a log-write web shell or an XMLDecoder payload. This leads to data theft and extortion.
entries.conditions: PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools 8.61 or 8.62 without Oracle's June 10 fix, with the PSIGW listening connector reachable and PSEMHUB deployed using the default allowedhosts.properties.
entries.mitigations: Apply Oracle's CVE-2026-35273 fix, disable or remove PSEMHUB if you cannot patch, do not treat path-based WAF blocking as a fix, and on suspected hosts preserve evidence, hunt for web shells and rotate all reachable credentials.

editorial.reason: ShinyHunters has exploited this PeopleSoft chain since May. It teaches two things that transfer: a default loopback allowlist turns server-side request forgery into unauthenticated RCE, and path-matching WAF rules fall to a single…

entries.title: OVHcloud CLI GitHub releases carried attacker binaries for 94 minutes, delivering GlassWorm
entries.summary: An attacker replaced the binaries on five OVHcloud CLI GitHub releases, kept them live for 94 minutes, then deleted the evidence. StepSecurity rebuilt the attacker's build, recovered the GlassWorm loader from an orphaned commit, and ran the full chain in isolation. Their replay shows the install.sh script never served arm64 Linux, Homebrew was not an infection path, and running the CLI's version command was enough to spot the malicious build.

lessons.point: Release assets can be swapped after publication and the evidence deleted, so a short exposure window can leave few traces.
lessons.excerpt: An attacker swapped the binaries on five OVHcloud CLI releases, stayed live for 94 minutes, and deleted the evidence.

lessons.point: Deleted malicious code could still be recovered from an orphaned commit, which made a full detonation possible.
lessons.excerpt: recovered the GlassWorm loader from an orphaned commit, and detonated the full chain in an isolated chamber

lessons.point: Exposure depends on install channel: Homebrew was not affected, and a simple version check identifies the bad build.
lessons.excerpt: Homebrew was never a path in, and a single ovhcloud version command was enough to spot the malicious build

entries.takeaway: Release binaries can be replaced after publication, so pin and verify checksums or provenance for downloaded CLIs instead of trusting the release tag.

actionable.title: Triage OVHcloud CLI installs and verify release-asset integrity
actionable.detail: On hosts and CI images that installed the OVHcloud CLI from GitHub releases or install.sh in the exposure window, run `ovhcloud version` and compare against the vendor's known-good build; treat Homebrew installs as unaffected per the replay. For all CLIs fetched from GitHub releases, pin a SHA-256 or verify signed provenance (e.g. artifact attestations) before execution rather than trusting the release tag.

entries.prior_art: Closest pool entry is the LiteLLM 1.107.0 trojanized PyPI/Docker release (built from a lookalike repo); release-asset swaps on GitHub are a known vector, but the reconstructed detonation and per-channel exposure analysis are new. Verifier: Release/tag tampering of trusted artifacts is well established (tj-actions/changed-files tag repoint 2025, Codecov bash uploader 2021, GlassWorm campaigns on OpenVSX/npm); the delta is a mutated GitHub release asset swap on a cloud vendor CLI plus a forensic replay recovering the loader from an orphaned commit.
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; the overstatements it flagged were corrected before merge.
entries.threat: Attacker with release-write access replaces signed-off binaries on existing GitHub releases with builds that drop the GlassWorm loader, then deletes traces.
entries.conditions: Users or CI pipelines that downloaded OVHcloud CLI binaries from the affected GitHub releases (or via install.sh on exposed platforms) during the 94-minute window.
entries.mitigations: Check the installed build with `ovhcloud version`; reinstall from a known-good release; pin checksums or verify provenance for release-asset downloads; restrict and monitor release-edit permissions.

editorial.reason: Live supply-chain incident: OVHcloud CLI release binaries swapped for 94 minutes to deliver GlassWorm; teaches release-asset verification and how to triage installs.

entries.title: Unit 42: CL-UNK-1211 hit government Linux servers with LLM-written payloads
entries.summary: Unit 42 tracked CL-UNK-1211 attacking government and state-affiliated Linux infrastructure from October 2025 to April 2026; payloads carried conversational, step-by-step reasoning comments, which suggests they were produced by an LLM or run by an AI agent. The attackers persisted by setting auto_prepend_file in every PHP config, stole passwords with a .bashrc sudo alias and a PHP login logger, and ran a Go RAT called SysGoRAT over WebSocket C2. They searched qmail mailboxes for social media account emails and tried to kill Cortex XDR processes. One dropped script had a syntax error and would have failed.
entries.takeaway: AI-assisted intrusions still rely on ordinary Linux tradecraft, so defenders should hunt for PHP config tampering, shell rc file aliases and outbound reverse shells, and can treat conversational reasoning comments inside dropped scripts as a triage signal.

lessons.point: LLM-generated payloads leave a fingerprint: conversational reasoning comments addressed to the operator, which can be used as a hunting and triage indicator.
lessons.excerpt: Multiple artifacts deployed throughout the intrusion contained AI-made conversational annotations and developer reasoning comments

lessons.point: Persistence came from editing auto_prepend_file in every PHP config, which loads a web shell before every PHP request. Monitor these directories for integrity changes.
lessons.excerpt: the attackers modified the auto_prepend_file value across all PHP configurations under the directories /etc/php/ and /opt/plesk/php/.

lessons.point: Credentials were harvested by a .bashrc sudo alias that fakes the password prompt, logs the password and then passes it to the real sudo.
lessons.excerpt: In one instance, they created an alias for the sudo command that was designed to execute each time a user attempted to run it.

lessons.point: The attackers planted fake red-team markers so responders would mistake the intrusion for an authorized security assessment.
lessons.excerpt: plant deceptive red-team markers to disguise activity as a legitimate security assessment

actionable.title: Hunt for CL-UNK-1211-style Linux persistence
actionable.detail: Search /etc/php/ and /opt/plesk/php/ for non-empty auto_prepend_file values. Look for sudo aliases or functions in users' .bashrc files. Check for files posing as vendor logs, such as Solarwinds.StatusLog.txt. Alert on php-fpm spawning shells or python3, and on mkfifo/nc, /dev/tcp and python socket reverse shells. Block 104.194.158.65. Enforce default-deny egress on web servers. Treat 'red team' markers found during an investigation as unverified until the engagement is confirmed.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: facts supported; flagged a plural overstatement about broken scripts (fixed to one script). Verifier novelty 42 (closest: Unit 42 TuxBot v3 LLM-assisted malware), relevance 80; took the lower novelty.
entries.prior_art: Closest pool entry is archive 'Measuring AI-enabled malware: ~97% of samples never reach production; AI changes how malware is authored, not how it executes'. This report is a concrete in-the-wild case consistent with that finding: the payloads were AI-authored, but the tradecraft is conventional and one script was broken. What is new is the specific TTP set (auto_prepend_file persistence, sudo-alias stealer, SysGoRAT, mailbox-to-social-media targeting, fake red-team markers). No earlier entry covers CL-UNK-1211 or SysGoRAT.
entries.threat: A state-interest espionage cluster gets into government Linux web and mail servers through web shells, keeps access with PHP config persistence and a Go RAT, steals credentials and mailboxes to take over social media accounts, dumps databases, and tampers with EDR and logs.
entries.conditions: Internet-facing Linux servers running PHP or Plesk and qmail, with cleartext credentials in config and history files, permissive outbound network access and EDR that can be killed by a local process.
entries.mitigations: Monitor PHP configuration and shell rc files for integrity changes, remove cleartext credentials from configs and history, enforce strict outbound firewall rules on servers, enable EDR tamper protection, forward logs off-host, and hunt for the published indicators.

editorial.reason: Live espionage campaign with LLM-written payloads and concrete Linux hunting leads (auto_prepend_file persistence, sudo-alias stealer).

entries.title: Datadog: 3,500+ RBAC bindings give dangerous permissions to groups like system:unauthenticated
entries.summary: Datadog analyzed 320,000+ bindings to the three Kubernetes built-in principals across 65,000 clusters from almost 10,000 organizations. After removing default bindings and 11,000 stale PodSecurityPolicy bindings (a feature removed in v1.25), 44,000 remained, and 3,500+ granted permissions Datadog classes as dangerous. Real exposure depends on the distribution: AKS rejects anonymous requests, EKS (v1.32+) and GKE (v1.35+) restrict anonymous endpoints, but GKE by default treats any valid Google account as system:authenticated.
entries.takeaway: Audit for any RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding to system:anonymous, system:unauthenticated or system:authenticated beyond the defaults, especially on GKE and in namespace-as-a-service clusters.

lessons.point: Dangerous grants to built-in principals are rare as a share but present at scale in real clusters.
lessons.excerpt: We found over 3,500 bindings that granted at least one of the permissions in that dangerous list.

lessons.point: On GKE, system:authenticated means anyone with a Google account unless blocked at cluster creation.
lessons.excerpt: by default it allows any user with a valid Google account to have that access to any GKE cluster.

lessons.point: Namespace admins in multi-tenant clusters can expose the whole cluster by binding to anonymous principals.
lessons.excerpt: a namespace-level admin can expose the overall cluster to risks by creating bindings to principals such as `system:unauthenticated`.

lessons.point: Distribution defaults decide whether anonymous bindings matter at all.
lessons.excerpt: AKS is one of the few distributions that uses the `--anonymous-auth=false` setting.

actionable.title: Find and remove bindings to Kubernetes built-in principals
actionable.detail: Run `kubectl get clusterrolebindings,rolebindings -A -o json` and flag subjects named system:anonymous, system:unauthenticated or system:authenticated other than the default system:basic-user, system:discovery and system:public-info-viewer bindings; review any that grant secrets read, pod create/exec, wildcard verbs/resources, bind/escalate/impersonate or node proxy. Set --anonymous-auth=false or the v1.34+ anonymous path allowlist on self-managed clusters, block arbitrary Google accounts on new GKE clusters, delete leftover podsecuritypolicy RBAC, and use admission policy to stop namespace admins from binding these principals.

entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim. Verifier: 'over 65,000' clusters; 'dangerous' is Datadog's own five-category definition. Verifier novelty 45.
entries.prior_art: Orca's 'Sys:All' research on GKE system:authenticated (cited in the post) and earlier internet scans for exposed anonymous Kubernetes APIs. This adds a large telemetry-based prevalence number across EKS, GKE and AKS rather than a new technique.
entries.threat: Anyone who can reach the API server (or, on GKE, anyone with a Google account) inherits permissions bound to built-in principals, which can include secret read or workload creation.
entries.conditions: Non-default bindings to system:anonymous/unauthenticated on distributions that allow anonymous access, or to system:authenticated where authentication is broad (GKE default).
entries.mitigations: Remove non-default bindings to built-in principals; disable or restrict anonymous auth; block arbitrary Google accounts on GKE; admission policies preventing such bindings; regular RBAC cleanup.

entries.title: CheckerBench gives agents 300 CVE-derived tasks to write static-analysis checkers
entries.summary: CheckerBench asks coding agents to write a working static-analysis checker for a known defect from start to finish inside a real repository. Each task comes with vulnerable and fixed revisions, a pinned analyzer environment and a scaffold. A companion framework, CheckerLab, rebuilds each submitted checker and scores it on whether it fires on the vulnerable version but not the fixed one, patch localization, false positives and tool use. Across 21 model-harness configurations the mean Pass@1 is 32.30% and the best is 45.33%.
entries.takeaway: Agents can sometimes turn a CVE into a reusable checker, but more than half of attempts fail, so treat agent-written SAST rules as drafts to validate on vulnerable/fixed pairs before shipping them to CI.

lessons.point: The benchmark is grounded in real CVEs across many CWEs and languages, not synthetic bugs.
lessons.excerpt: 300 tasks derived from 297 CVEs across 167 repositories, 85 CWEs, and five language ecosystems

lessons.point: Scoring checks that the checker fires on vulnerable code and stays quiet on the fix, plus its false-positive rate. That is the right acceptance test for any generated rule.
lessons.excerpt: measures vulnerable-fixed diagnostic contrast, patch localization, false positives, and tool use

lessons.point: Current agents mostly fail. Even the best configuration passes fewer than half the tasks.
lessons.excerpt: Across 21 model-harness configurations and three independent repeats per configuration, mean Pass@1 is 32.30%, while the best reaches 45.33%

actionable.title: Gate agent-written SAST checkers on vulnerable/fixed contrast
actionable.detail: When using an agent to turn a CVE or bug report into a CodeQL, Semgrep or analyzer-specific checker, require it to fire on the vulnerable commit and stay silent on the fixed commit. Also require it to stay under a false-positive budget on a clean corpus before the rule goes into CI. Expect less than 50% first-try success and budget for iteration or human repair.

entries.verify_note: No problems found; excerpts verbatim. Verifier novelty 60.
entries.prior_art: CVE-based agent benchmarks such as CyberGym, SEC-bench and CVE-Bench measure patching, PoC generation or detection. LLM-assisted CodeQL and Semgrep rule-generation papers exist but lacked a large executable benchmark. CheckerBench is new in scoring end-to-end checker synthesis with rebuilds and vulnerable/fixed contrast.

entries.title: F5 BIG-IP APM pre-auth heap overflow RCE (CVE-2026-94127) is exploited
entries.summary: watchTowr Labs patch-diffed F5's fix for CVE-2026-94127 (advisory K000162605), an unauthenticated heap overflow in BIG-IP APM's traffic manager (tmm) that F5 reports as exploited in the wild. When an APM OAuth profile is configured, the HTTP Authorization header was copied into a fixed-size heap buffer with no length check, so an oversized header on an OAuth endpoint corrupts memory and, per the researchers, leads to remote code execution despite ASLR, NX and SELinux. Affected: BIG-IP APM 21.1.0, 17.5.0-17.5.1 and 17.1.0-17.1.3; other modules and BIG-IQ are not affected.

lessons.point: The root cause is a decades-old bug class: an attacker-controlled HTTP header was copied into a fixed-size heap buffer without a length check, and the fix only adds that check. Any code path that parses credentials before authentication needs explicit bounds checks.
lessons.excerpt: It is simple: before the patch, there was no size check before copying the value to the heap buffer, and now there is one.

lessons.point: The bug sits on an edge appliance that terminates TLS and brokers authentication, so a pre-auth memory-corruption flaw there exposes plaintext traffic and credentials. Patch it as an emergency.
lessons.excerpt: In other words, it lives at the very edge of your network, terminates your TLS, sees all of your traffic in plaintext, and holds the keys to your authentication.

lessons.point: The vendor advisory reported in-the-wild exploitation before the public technical analysis came out, so patch timelines should assume attackers are already using it.
lessons.excerpt: Even more scary, though: this wasn't just any vulnerability. There were bad people on the Internet exploiting it.

entries.takeaway: Edge appliances keep shipping pre-auth memory-corruption bugs in authentication paths (here, a missing length check on an Authorization header), so they need emergency patching, minimal exposure and crash-based detection.

actionable.title: Apply F5 K000162605 hotfixes on BIG-IP APM with OAuth profiles and hunt for compromise
actionable.detail: Find BIG-IP systems running APM 21.1.0, 17.5.0-17.5.1 or 17.1.0-17.1.3, especially those with an APM OAuth profile on a virtual server, and apply the engineering hotfixes in F5 advisory K000162605. Because the flaw was exploited in the wild, also hunt for compromise. Look for unexpected tmm crashes or restarts and for requests to /f5-oauth2/ endpoints with abnormally large Authorization headers. Check the integrity of the tmm crash hook script (/etc/bigstart/scripts/tmm.finish), which the researchers abused to get command execution. Until the patch is in, limit who can reach the OAuth endpoints.

entries.prior_art: watchTowr Citrix NetScaler pre-auth heap overflow CVE-2026-8452; Kemp LoadMaster pre-auth RCE CVE-2026-8037.
entries.threat: An unauthenticated remote attacker can get code execution on the BIG-IP traffic manager (tmm), which sees decrypted traffic and handles authentication.
entries.conditions: BIG-IP APM on an affected version with an OAuth profile configured on a reachable virtual server.
entries.mitigations: Apply the K000162605 hotfixes, limit exposure of the OAuth endpoints, monitor for tmm crashes and oversized Authorization headers, and check the integrity of tmm.finish.

issues: mild: sentence_words 46 > 45 (When an APM OAuth profile is configured, the HTTP Authorization header was copied into a fixed-size heap buffer with no )

editorial.reason: Pre-auth RCE in an internet-facing BIG-IP edge appliance, exploited in the wild; teaches emergency patching and minimal exposure for auth-path parsing on edge devices.

entries.title: GitHub Security Lab's Fuzzing Taskflow has an LLM agent write AFL++ harnesses
entries.summary: GitHub Security Lab released a Fuzzing Taskflow that takes a C/C++ GitHub repo and autonomously writes fuzzing harnesses, runs AFL++, reads coverage to chase gaps, improves the harnesses, and triages crashes into reports. The agent makes decisions while MCP tools do the execution, and a coverage loop with doubling time budgets stops once gains plateau. The author warns that the agent runs LLM-chosen build commands on the host with no container. It should only run in a throwaway environment, and its crash verdicts still need human review.

lessons.point: Split authority: the LLM picks what to fuzz and which gap to chase, while narrow tools perform execution and state lives in a database rather than in the agent.
lessons.excerpt: the **LLM agent owns the decisions, and the MCP tools own the execution**

lessons.point: Bound agent compute with plateau detection: stop iterating when coverage gains fall below a small threshold for two rounds.
lessons.excerpt: once two consecutive iterations each gain less than a configurable threshold (1% absolute line coverage by default)

lessons.point: Coverage-driven dictionary enrichment pulls magic constants from the comparisons that guard unreached code, helping the fuzzer pass hard checks.
lessons.excerpt: Then, after every coverage step, the pipeline looks at the guards near the uncovered lines

lessons.point: An agent that runs LLM-chosen build commands on the host is a prompt-injection risk; contain it in a disposable environment.
lessons.excerpt: A prompt-injected agent could, in principle, do anything your user can.

entries.takeaway: LLM agents can now take over the labor-intensive parts of fuzzing (harness writing, coverage chasing, triage), but they need containment and human review of verdicts.

actionable.title: Run seclab-taskflows-fuzzing against a C/C++ project in a Codespace
actionable.detail: Start a Codespace from github.com/GitHubSecurityLab/seclab-taskflows-fuzzing and run ./scripts/fuzzing/run_fuzzing.sh owner/repo (try DaveGamble/cJSON first as a smoke test). Do not run it on a workstation with credentials or elevated privileges. Watch the dashboard on port 8765, and treat every 'vulnerability' verdict and suggested diff as a draft to confirm by hand.

entries.prior_art: GitHub Security Lab Taskflow Android audit (24 vulnerabilities); OSS-Fuzz-gen.
entries.threat: The agent executes arbitrary LLM-chosen build commands on the host; a prompt-injected agent (for example via hostile content in the target repo) could act with the user's privileges.
entries.conditions: Running the taskflow outside a disposable environment, or with elevated privileges.
entries.mitigations: Run only in a Codespace or throwaway VM without elevated privileges; keep human review on verdicts and suggested patches.

entries.title: Next.js has unauthenticated RCE in use cache functions returning typed arrays
entries.summary: A critical GHSA for npm/next reports that apps using the App Router with Cache Components can be driven to remote code execution when a `use cache` function returns multiple typed arrays, with no known workaround short of upgrading. The fetched advisory page captured only the CVSS boilerplate, so the details here come from the GHSA feed summary alone.

lessons.point: The vulnerable surface is the cache serialization path for typed arrays in App Router Cache Components.
lessons.excerpt: The application needs to have a `use cache` function that returns multiple typed arrays.

lessons.point: There is no configuration workaround; affected apps must upgrade.
lessons.excerpt: There is no known workaround for affected applications

entries.takeaway: Upgrade Next.js now if any `use cache` function returns typed arrays; there is no workaround.

actionable.title: Find `use cache` functions returning typed arrays
actionable.detail: Grep for 'use cache' in App Router code, check return values for Uint8Array/Float32Array etc., and upgrade Next.js to the patched release.

entries.prior_art: React Server Components serialization RCE (React2Shell, CVE-2025-55182) is the closest prior class: framework-level serialization of server data leading to RCE.
entries.verify_note: Advisory body not captured (fetched page holds only CVSS boilerplate); lessons rest on the GHSA feed summary.

entries.title: Wiz CIRT describes what an AI-driven cloud intrusion looks like
entries.summary: Wiz CIRT walks through intrusions where an AI agent system ran the whole operation across cloud, Kubernetes, CI/CD, identity and databases at once. It lists eight traits that separate these from human or scripted attacks, such as hundreds or thousands of actions per hour, credential chaining across platforms, self-repairing scripts, pentest-style naming, task IDs in resource names and heavily commented code. The footprint is loud but split across logs, so no single alert tells the story.

lessons.point: Tempo and absence of working-hour patterns separate agents from human operators.
lessons.excerpt: Activity can reach hundreds or thousands of actions per hour and continues for long periods without the pauses or working-hour patterns typical of a human operator.

lessons.point: Credentials chain across platforms because the agent speaks every platform's API.
lessons.excerpt: Because the agent has native fluency across so many technologies, every credential becomes a stepping stone to the next platform.

lessons.point: Failed attempts are fixed in minutes, so a blocked first try tells you little.
lessons.excerpt: If an attempt fails, the agent immediately reads the error, rewrites its script on the fly, and tries again within minutes

lessons.point: Names like pentest, recon and exfil are an observable tell and a likely guardrail bypass.
lessons.excerpt: Resources, files, and payloads created by the actor are consistently labeled with terms such as `pentest`, `probe`, `recon`, `redteam`, and `exfil`.

lessons.point: The problem is fragmentation, not stealth.
lessons.excerpt: The challenge for defenders isn't that these attacks are invisible.

entries.takeaway: Detect AI-driven intrusions by correlating identity, cloud, CI/CD and workload logs and by hunting the agent's tells.

actionable.title: Hunt the agent's tells
actionable.detail: Add detections for resource names containing pentest, probe, recon, redteam or exfil; numeric task-ID suffixes (-b, -c retries); and bursts of cross-platform API calls from one source. Join identity provider, cloud audit, CI/CD and cluster logs on one timeline.

entries.prior_art: CrowdStrike and Microsoft reports describe attacker use of agent frameworks; this is the first defender-side field guide of observable traits in the pools. Verifier: Sysdig's AI-assisted AWS intrusion write-up (2026), Anthropic GTG-1002, Wiz/Unit42 agentic-attack notes. Delta is the codified 8-trait tell list from a multi-pl
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every claim supported by the source.

editorial.reason: Field guide to observable traits of AI-driven cloud intrusions from real investigations.

entries.title: Wiz lists the fingerprints that mark an intrusion as agent-driven
entries.summary: Wiz reviews public agentic intrusions (ARTEX, Hermes, PentestGPT-derived harnesses and Claude Code workflows) and three of its own cases. The three are an exposed Flowise instance turned into a mass-exploitation node, a Java gateway RCE that swept 602 steps across 12 technique families, and an MCP-interface command injection that led to bulk secret and Kubernetes token theft. Wiz distills fingerprints of agent activity: machine-paced iteration whose cadence varies with step complexity, natural-language plans inside scripts, versioned self-correcting tooling, breadth-first technique coverage, noisy parallel lateral movement, and probe-before-payload discipline.

lessons.point: Cadence is a tell: gaps between steps vary with how complex each step is, unlike fixed-interval beacons or millisecond auto-exploit chains, and it continues for many hours without fatigue gaps.
lessons.excerpt: The tell is a variable cadence that tracks step complexity

lessons.point: Agent-generated tooling carries written plans and rationale, which can even name the agent framework.
lessons.excerpt: Scripts and artifacts that carry written rationale (attack plans, explanations of what and why).

lessons.point: Agents read errors and rewrite their approach across numbered script versions, so blocking one path does not stop the intrusion.
lessons.excerpt: A static playbook cannot read an AWS error and re-derive the regional-STS requirement.

lessons.point: Agents try many lateral paths in parallel and keep going without regard to noise, which gives defenders a detection opportunity if signals are correlated.
lessons.excerpt: The loudness is itself a detection opportunity.

entries.takeaway: Agent-driven intrusions are loud and leave readable rationale, so behavioral detections built on cadence, commented /tmp scripts, versioned retries and parallel lateral sweeps can catch them.

actionable.title: Hunt for agentic-intrusion fingerprints in workload telemetry
actionable.detail: Write detections for: (1) many distinct new scripts in /tmp on one workload over hours, appearing about every one to two minutes; (2) scripts with natural-language plan headers or heavy comments; (3) versioned file ladders (x, x2, x3) following 401/403 errors; (4) metadata-endpoint fallback sequences (IMDSv2, then IMDSv1, then ECS credentials, then IPv6 IMDS); (5) parallel port and host sweeps from one workload. Correlate them across identity, cloud and Kubernetes logs rather than alerting on each alone.

entries.verify_note: Verifier upheld all four lessons; incremental over GTG-1002 and earlier Wiz/Microsoft agentic-attack reports (novelty 30 vs 42, lower kept).
entries.prior_art: Wiz CIRT's own 'Anatomy of AI-Driven Cloud Attacks' (2026-10-19, already pooled) listed eight similar traits (tempo, self-repairing scripts, heavy comments); Microsoft's Storm-0940/ARTEX report and the Unit 42 AI-assisted attack investigation. This post adds three new cases and sharper criteria (cadence varying with step complexity, probe-before-payload).
entries.threat: Attackers using agent harnesses that write custom tooling, adapt to errors and escalate from one exposed service to cloud credential theft, Kubernetes token theft, lateral movement and bulk secret exfiltration.
entries.conditions: Internet-exposed services such as unauthenticated Flowise endpoints, Java RCE on gateways, or MCP interfaces that accept attacker-controlled commands, running on workloads with reachable metadata endpoints and Kubernetes service-account tokens.
entries.mitigations: Remove unauthenticated exposure of agent-builder and MCP endpoints, restrict metadata and service-account token access from workloads, and build behavioral detections on script cadence, commented generated tooling, versioned retries and parallel sweeps, correlated across identity, endpoint and cloud signals.

entries.title: Google: eight eMudhra CA keys had weak entropy and Chrome blocked them
entries.summary: On October 17, 2026 Google's Chrome Root Program got a report that private keys for eight eMudhra subordinate CA certificates were generated with insufficient randomness, which would let anyone forge trusted HTTPS certificates. Chrome blocked the keys by public-key hash within about 100 minutes, with no browser update needed. No certificates from the intermediates were logged to Certificate Transparency before the block. Chrome will also remove the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 root.

lessons.point: Weak entropy means anyone can derive the CA keys and forge certificates for any site.
lessons.excerpt: The private keys for these certificates were generated with insufficient randomness (i.e., weak cryptographic entropy), enabling anyone to forge trusted HTTPS certificates to impersonate any website

lessons.point: A key-hash block protected users immediately, with no update.
lessons.excerpt: Chrome users were immediately protected against all certificates sharing those keys, without requiring a browser update or restart.

lessons.point: Certificate Transparency enforcement limited the damage window.
lessons.excerpt: no fraudulent certificates issued by these CAs could have been used against CT-enforcing clients.

lessons.point: Site operators must move off the removed root before the Chrome Root Store change.
lessons.excerpt: must immediately acquire and install a new TLS certificate from another PKI hierarchy

entries.takeaway: Weak randomness in CA key generation is catastrophic; Certificate Transparency and fast key-hash blocks are what contained this one.

actionable.title: Check your chains for emSign ECC G3
actionable.detail: Inventory certificates that chain to emSign ECC Root CA - G3, replace them from another root before the Chrome Root Store change lands, and keep CT monitoring on your domains.

entries.prior_art: Past CA incidents (DigiNotar, Symantec) involve compromise or mis-issuance; a weak-entropy intermediate key set blocked in hours is a distinct case. Verifier: Debian OpenSSL weak-key incident (2008); Trustico/DigiCert key-exposure revocation (2018); Symantec and Entrust distrust. Delta: SPKI-hash CRLSet block within ~
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every claim supported by the source.

editorial.reason: Weak-entropy CA keys blocked by Chrome within hours; root removal scheduled.

entries.title: 333 Tor exit relays hijacked with the Ebury backdoor to intercept SSH
entries.summary: A researcher who goes by kaba found that attackers had taken over about 333 Tor exit relays (roughly 10% of exits) and set them to redirect SSH on port 22 to 12 interception servers, stealing passwords, watching sessions and infecting the real server with Ebury. They had gained access to the servers in August and deployed Ebury 1.8.3 on them. Tor's network health team flagged the relays as bad exits on October 4 and all were offline by October 5. The attack also favored unencrypted mail traffic.

lessons.point: SSH on port 22 was silently redirected to attacker servers on infected exits.
lessons.excerpt: if you attempt an SSH connection over Port 22, you're unknowingly redirected to one of 12 SSH interception servers.

lessons.point: The infection started two months earlier with a Linux credential-stealing backdoor.
lessons.excerpt: The attackers had gained access to the servers two months earlier, in August, and quietly deployed their Ebury 1.8.3 payload (an OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer for Linux).

lessons.point: Scale: roughly a tenth of Tor's exit capacity.
lessons.excerpt: To give you a sense of scale, all of Tor has around 3000 exit relays, so roughly 10% were under their control.

lessons.point: A victim who ignored the host-key warning also got their server infected.
lessons.excerpt: Opens a second connection to your server and infects it with Ebury

entries.takeaway: Never accept a changed SSH host key over Tor or any untrusted path; use key auth, and expect backdoored infrastructure hosts to be turned into traffic interceptors.

actionable.title: Treat host-key changes as incidents
actionable.detail: Use SSH keys instead of passwords (especially over anonymizing networks), pin host keys, never click through changed-key warnings, and scan relay or bastion hosts for Ebury indicators.

entries.prior_art: Malicious Tor exit relays are a known threat (sslstrip, bitcoin-swapping); mass port-22 redirection with a backdoored relay fleet is new. Verifier: Malicious Tor exit sniffing/sslstrip (Josh Pitts 2014, 'Spoiled Onions' 2016, KAX17 relays 2020-21); ESET Ebury research (Windigo 2014, 2024 report)
entries.verify_note: Independent fresh-context verifier re-read the source; discrepancies it found (title/summary overstatements) were corrected before merge.

entries.title: Datadog's pathrunner automates 80+ AWS IAM privilege-escalation paths for defenders
entries.author: Seth Art
entries.summary: Datadog released pathrunner, a modular Metasploit-style framework that exploits the AWS IAM privilege-escalation paths catalogued in pathfinding.cloud, with identity import/switching, multiple payloads per module, managed 'attacker' infrastructure and a workspace report. The report lists the resources created and the CloudTrail events pathrunner expects to have triggered, turning a red-team run into a detection-engineering checklist. It is incremental over Pacu and Stratus Red Team; its value is the per-payload detection coverage it enables.

lessons.point: In cloud environments lateral movement is mostly identity-to-identity via credentials, so model attack paths as IAM graphs, not network hops.
lessons.excerpt: more often than not, penetration testers and real attacks are hopping from one cloud identity to another by accessing credentials

lessons.point: The tool ships a broad catalogue of exploit modules mapped to required permissions.
lessons.excerpt: As of October 2026, there are over 80 exploit modules in pathrunner.

lessons.point: Write detections per payload, not per single post-exploitation action: a detection for 'create admin user' is blind when the attacker picks another payload.
lessons.excerpt: if you walk through each and every pathrunner payload in your environment and build detections for each of them, you will have a much greater chance of catching malicious activity

lessons.point: The workspace report gives the blue team the CloudTrail events the run is expected to generate (Datadog's expectation, not a verified log) to check detections against.
lessons.excerpt: the report includes a table that lists all of the CloudTrail events that we think pathrunner would have triggered

lessons.point: Demonstrated exploitability is the triage signal for misconfigurations, as a public PoC is for CVEs.
lessons.excerpt: An offensive tool demonstrates the impact of an attack, enabling defenders to prioritize exploitable misconfigurations based on how impactful they are.

entries.takeaway: Run pathrunner in a sandbox (Pathfinding Labs) and use its CloudTrail report to test that every payload, not just one, trips a detection.

actionable.title: Detection coverage drill with pathrunner
actionable.detail: Deploy Pathfinding Labs in a sandbox account, run each pathrunner module with every payload, export `workspace report`, and diff the expected CloudTrail events against what your SIEM alerted on; file a detection gap per miss.

entries.prior_art: Pacu, Rhino Security's AWS escalation methods/CloudGoat, Stratus Red Team (per-technique detection testing), and Datadog's own pathfinding.cloud and Pathfinding Labs.
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier: all excerpts verbatim; novelty 40->35 (incremental over Pacu/Stratus); CloudTrail table is expected, not verified, events.

entries.title: UAT-11985 lured Taiwan researchers with likely AI-templated invitations and live MFA relay
entries.summary: Cisco Talos tracked a mid-2026 advanced persistent threat (APT) spear-phishing campaign against Taiwan research staff. It reused real public events, faked senders at the Taiwan European Union Centre, the NCCU Institute of International Relations and the Taiwan Research Institute, and used near-identical three-part templates that Talos assesses were likely AI-assisted. Links displayed as Google Forms led to a fake Google sign-in, and event posters carried swapped QR codes to catch anyone who scanned a printed copy. The kit is operator-driven: HTTP POST sends the victim's identifier, password and browser fingerprint to the actor, who relays them to real Google; a WebSocket channel then tells the page which MFA or passkey screen to render, giving full session takeover. Talos assesses with moderate confidence that the kit's UI was written in Simplified Chinese first.
entries.takeaway: Real-time relay kits defeat OTP and push MFA; only origin-bound factors (passkeys, security keys) stop this class, and lure quality is no longer a usable tell.

lessons.point: Lure uniformity across topics points to template-driven, probably LLM-assisted generation; polish no longer signals legitimacy.
lessons.excerpt: suggesting the content was generated from a reusable prompt template rather than independently authored

lessons.point: Swapped QR codes on genuine posters extend reach to people who never got the email, and bypass email link scanning.
lessons.excerpt: While the poster designs were scraped from legitimate websites, the embedded QR codes were maliciously altered.

lessons.point: A live operator drives the victim's page step by step, mirroring whatever challenge Google actually issues.
lessons.excerpt: The C2 server streams real-time instructions to the phishing page via this channel, dictating exactly which MFA challenge screen to render.

lessons.point: The goal is a complete authenticated session, so non-phishing-resistant MFA gives no protection.
lessons.excerpt: This mechanism effectively bypasses multi-factor authentication (MFA) to harvest complete, authenticated session tokens.

actionable.title: Enforce phishing-resistant MFA for research and policy staff, and hunt for the kit
actionable.detail: Enroll targeted staff in passkeys or hardware security keys (Google Advanced Protection where possible), since a relayed password-plus-OTP or push flow yields a full session. Deploy the Talos ClamAV signature Html.Phishing.UAT11985-10060614-0 and Snort SIDs 1:67198 / 7:31, ingest the IOCs from Cisco-Talos/IOCs 2026/10/uat-11985.txt, and tell staff to register for events only via the organizer's own site, not links or QR codes in unsolicited invitations or posters.

entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim; AI involvement correctly hedged. Verifier: 'bypass email link scanning' (lesson 2) is not in the source. Verifier novelty 40.
entries.prior_art: Real-time AitM relay kits (Evilginx, Tycoon 2FA and others) and Talos's own JWR phishing framework write-up with similar WebSocket use are established. New here: an operator-driven Google kit that also branches on passkey availability, QR-altered event posters as a physical second vector, likely AI-templated lures against Taiwan researchers, and localization-based attribution of the kit's developer.
entries.threat: Targeted credential and session theft of Google accounts belonging to Taiwan research and policy staff.
entries.conditions: Victim follows a disguised registration link or scans a modified poster QR code and authenticates with a password plus a relayable second factor.
entries.mitigations: Phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys or FIDO2 keys); verify invitations with the named institution through a known channel; Talos ClamAV/Snort coverage and published IOCs; link-rewrite and QR-aware email scanning.

entries.title: watchTowr turns Citrix NetScaler DTLS overflow (CVE-2026-88772) into RCE
entries.summary: NetScaler's DTLS reassembly trusts fragment_length=1 to mark a message complete but keeps nearly the whole record in its buffer chain. After 120 such records, the copy routine writes about 174 KB into a fixed 35,840-byte scratch buffer with no size check. Because the nsppe binary has no PIE, no RELRO and no stack canary, watchTowr repaired a clobbered pointer, faked an object's method table and used a ROP chain to mprotect and run shellcode, all before any login.

lessons.point: The bug is reachable before authentication on a default setting: DTLS is on for VPN virtual servers unless explicitly disabled, and it was exploited as a zero-day.
lessons.excerpt: It requires DTLS to be enabled which is the default on VPN virtual servers unless an administrator explicitly set `-dtls OFF` and was exploited in the wild as a zero-day.

lessons.point: Root cause is a parser that uses one length field to walk the record and a different one to track reassembly, so the two disagree about how much data was kept.
lessons.excerpt: NSPPE uses `length=120` to find the hidden header, but it uses `fragment_length=1` when rebuilding `message_seq=2`.

lessons.point: The final sink is an unchecked memcpy loop into a fixed-size buffer; the patch only adds a remaining-space check per chunk.
lessons.excerpt: The vulnerable function then copies that entire chain into the 35,840-byte scratch buffer without checking whether it fits.

lessons.point: The DTLS cookie exchange is anti-spoofing, not authentication, so it does not shrink the pre-auth attack surface.
lessons.excerpt: This only proves that the client can receive packets at its IP address; it does not authenticate a user.

lessons.point: One bug in the same bulletin is not fixed by upgrading alone and needs a configuration change.
lessons.excerpt: Fixed by enabling Enhanced ISN Generation, not by the upgrade alone.

entries.takeaway: Patch NetScaler to 14.1-73.37 / 13.1-64.23 or later now, or set -dtls OFF on VPN virtual servers until you can, and enable Enhanced ISN Generation separately.

actionable.title: Patch or disable DTLS on NetScaler Gateway VPN virtual servers
actionable.detail: Upgrade NetScaler ADC/Gateway to 14.1-73.37, 13.1-64.23 (or the listed FIPS/NDcPP builds) or later. If you cannot patch immediately, set -dtls OFF on VPN virtual servers (the DTLS listener). Enable Enhanced ISN Generation for CVE-2026-88778. Use watchTowr's public detection artefact generator to check exposure, and treat appliances that were exposed before patching as possibly compromised. For protocol code you own, add tests where declared fragment lengths disagree with bytes on the wire.

entries.prior_art: Close sibling in archive.json: watchTowr's Citrix NetScaler pre-auth heap overflow CVE-2026-8452 (unchecked fixed-size buffer copy during SAML canonicalization). Same appliance, same unchecked-copy class, same exploitation write-up style; the delta is the DTLS fragment-reassembly length confusion and the no-PIE .bss exploitation path. Verifier's closest: watchTowr Citrix NetScaler pre-auth heap overflow CVE-2026-8452 (SAML canonicalization).
entries.verify_note: Verifier: numbers, fixed builds and excerpts match; an unsupported 'port 443' claim in the actionable was removed.
entries.threat: Unauthenticated remote code execution on the NetScaler packet engine over UDP DTLS.
entries.conditions: NetScaler ADC/Gateway before the fixed builds with DTLS enabled on a VPN virtual server (the default).
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to fixed builds; disable DTLS as a stopgap; enable Enhanced ISN Generation; hunt for compromise on exposed appliances.

entries.title: Authlib accepts a JSON web signature with no signatures as verified
entries.summary: Authlib before 1.9.0 returns the payload of a JSON Web Signature (JWS) object in JSON serialization as verified when its `signatures` array is empty. The validity flag starts as true and only the per-signature loop can clear it, so an empty list skips every check. Any service that calls `JsonWebSignature.deserialize_json()` on outside input accepts a forged payload, even when it passes the correct key; upgrade to 1.9.0.

lessons.point: The bug is a fail-open default: the validity flag starts true and only the loop body can clear it, so zero signatures means zero checks.
lessons.excerpt: `is_valid` is initialised to `True` and only ever set to `False` from inside the loop.

lessons.point: Holding the correct key does not protect the caller, because no signature is ever examined.
lessons.excerpt: and [B] shows that holding the correct key does not

lessons.point: Normal tests still pass, so the flaw hides in a deployment that looks healthy.
lessons.excerpt: [C] proves the verifier works normally on a genuine object, so a deployment looks healthy.

entries.takeaway: Any verifier that loops over signatures must reject an empty list; test your JWS and JWT code for that case.

actionable.title: Add an empty-signatures test to every signature verifier
actionable.detail: Upgrade Authlib to 1.9.0 or move to joserfc. In your own token and multi-signature verifiers, add a negative test that submits a JSON-serialized token with `"signatures": []` and a forged payload, with and without the real key, and require a rejection. Search for validity flags set to true before a loop.

entries.verify_note: Verifier confirmed the core bug; it noted the 1.9.0 fix is inferred from the release reference and rated novelty 30 (known fail-open class).
entries.prior_art: Fail-open signature checks such as JWT alg=none bypasses are a known bug class; this is a new instance in Authlib's JWS JSON path, not a new technique.
entries.threat: An unauthenticated remote attacker forges identity or authorization claims that the relying party accepts as signed.
entries.conditions: A service calls Authlib's JsonWebSignature.deserialize_json() on input it did not produce, with Authlib before 1.9.0.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to Authlib 1.9.0 or joserfc, and reject JWS objects whose signatures array is empty.

editorial.reason: Critical authentication bypass in a widely used Python library; the fail-open empty-loop pattern is a test every verifier should have.

entries.title: Next.js Image Optimization has unauthenticated RCE via SVG through sharp
entries.summary: A critical GHSA for npm/next reports that a memory-related bug in an upstream library used by Next.js Image Optimization can lead to remote code execution when SVG files are processed on glibc-based Linux; the workaround is to ensure the sharp version Next.js uses is new enough. lessons.excerpt: A memory-related vulnerability has been discovered in an upstream library used for Image Optimization can lead to possible remote code execution (RCE) when Next.js runs on glibc-based Linux.

lessons.point: The fix is a transitive dependency bump: pin a patched sharp.
lessons.excerpt: Ensure the version of `sharp` used by Next.js is greater

entries.takeaway: Pin a patched sharp under Next.js and consider disabling SVG optimization; image pipelines are unauthenticated RCE surface.

actionable.title: Check the sharp version Next.js resolves
actionable.detail: Run npm ls sharp in each Next.js app, upgrade to the patched sharp, and keep dangerouslyAllowSVG off unless required.

entries.title: Wiz: Gheist used stolen GitHub tokens to dump secrets through Actions logs
entries.summary: Wiz Research tracked Gheist, active from September 15 and still running on October 24, which used stolen GitHub tokens to push more than 13,500 branches across more than 850 accounts, each adding a `sync-check` workflow that tries to print the repository's secrets into its own log. The tool downloads the log through the GitHub API and deletes the run seconds later, so no attacker domain is involved. GitHub's July safeguard covers only public repositories; Wiz saw private enterprise repositories hit and, within hours, the same organization's cloud credentials used to list AWS Secrets Manager.

lessons.point: Secrets leave through GitHub's own API, so blocking outbound traffic does not help; detection has to use workflow and audit events.
lessons.excerpt: Because the secrets leave through GitHub's own API, there is no attacker domain or outbound connection to block

lessons.point: GitHub's public-repository safeguard does not apply once an enterprise credential is stolen.
lessons.excerpt: once an enterprise credential is compromised, that control doesn’t apply

lessons.point: Wiz gives concrete hunt indicators: short-lived workflow runs on ci-sync branches.
lessons.excerpt: workflow runs on "ci-sync-*" branches that were deleted within a minute of completion

lessons.point: Cloudsmith's security head notes that a token issued to a person months earlier still carried full write access.
lessons.excerpt: a credential issued to a human months ago still carried full write authority

entries.takeaway: A stolen GitHub token turns your own CI into a secrets-theft channel, so hunt for the sync-check pattern and replace long-lived personal access tokens with short-lived, scoped ones.

actionable.title: Hunt for Gheist workflows and shorten token lifetimes
actionable.detail: Search organization audit logs for branches named ci-sync- plus six characters that only add .github/workflows/sync-check.yml with the commit message "ci: sync config", workflow runs deleted within a minute, and API calls with the user agent "gheist". Rotate every secret those repositories hold, then replace personal access tokens with GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens and require reviewers on environments with production secrets.

entries.verify_note: Core claims supported via Dark Reading's write-up of Wiz; the workflow 'tries' to print secrets and the long-lived-token point is a Cloudsmith quote, both now worded so. Novelty lowered to its 40.
entries.prior_art: Secrets-dumping workflows pushed with stolen tokens appeared in earlier campaigns such as GhostAction; Gheist adds log-then-delete theft with no attacker domain and reaches private enterprise repositories past GitHub's public-repository safeguard.
entries.threat: Theft of repository and cloud secrets through malicious GitHub Actions workflows pushed with stolen tokens, followed by cloud enumeration.
entries.conditions: A GitHub token, often from infostealer malware or an earlier supply chain compromise, with write access to repositories that hold secrets.
entries.mitigations: Hunt for the ci-sync and sync-check indicators, rotate exposed secrets, use GitHub Apps or short-lived fine-grained tokens, and require reviewers on production environments.
