entries.title: Google declines to fix zero-click SMS that crashes Android telephony
entries.summary: A malformed WAP (Wireless Application Protocol) Push data SMS makes WapPushOverSms.decodeWapPdu() cast an unchecked header length to a negative int and allocate a negative-size array, killing com.android.phone and dropping active calls, including emergency calls, with no user interaction or visible message. Rapid repeated sends (about 30) corrupt the SQLite SMS store so the phone crashes on every boot, and carrier redelivery re-triggers it even after a factory reset. Google's Android and Devices VRP (Vulnerability Reward Program) closed it as Won't Fix, non-security, with no CVE, and the researcher published a working proof of concept and a one-line bounds-check fix.

lessons.point: The payload arrives as a data SMS that never appears in the inbox, so the victim sees no message and no sender number.
lessons.excerpt: The message is delivered as a data SMS and is never shown to the user

lessons.point: Carrier redelivery of unacknowledged messages turns one crash into repeated outages, and a factory reset alone does not stop it.
lessons.excerpt: because the carrier re-sends the unacknowledged payload and re-triggers the crash

lessons.point: A single message caused intermittent outages for up to a week in the researcher's own testing.
lessons.excerpt: a single message caused intermittent outages for up to a week in testing

lessons.point: The vendor triage outcome was non-security across several tickets, so defenders cannot rely on a patch or CVE and must treat this as an unfixed exposure.
lessons.excerpt: Across three tickets and four engineers, Google classified it as a non-security issue.

entries.takeaway: Any Android device reachable by SMS can be knocked off telephony, emergency calling included, and the vendor treats it as a non-security bug with no fix scheduled.

actionable.title: Track carrier and OEM mitigations for the WAP Push crash
actionable.detail: For managed Android fleets, ask carriers whether they filter malformed WAP Push data SMS on port 2948 and ask OEMs whether they ship the bounds check in WapPushOverSms before the cast. For recovery, the source says moving the physical SIM to a non-Android device stops carrier redelivery, then the SMS records are cleared over ADB (Android Debug Bridge). When auditing parsers, flag any long-to-int cast used as an allocation size without a range check.

entries.verify_note: Verifier upheld all four lessons; outage duration is the researcher's own test claim (novelty 50 vs 70, lower kept; prior art Stagefright and SMS-of-death crashes).
entries.prior_art: No equivalent pool entry. The pool's Android items (GitHub Security Lab's 24 Android vulnerabilities, the Qualcomm zero-day in the March 2026 update) cover other bugs. Earlier SMS-of-death style crashes exist as a bug class, but this one's persistence through database corruption and carrier redelivery, and the vendor's won't-fix outcome, are specific to it.
entries.threat: A remote attacker who knows only the victim's phone number can silently crash Android telephony, drop calls including emergency calls, and with about 20 to 30 messages leave the device persistently without telephony.
entries.conditions: Android devices whose WapPushOverSms casts the WAP Push header length without a range check. The source reports a 100% reproduction rate on a Pixel 9 on April 2026 firmware and several Samsung Galaxy and A-series models. The vendor issued no fix and no CVE.
entries.mitigations: Add a range check on the header length before the cast in WapPushOverSms.java (the source's proposed fix), carrier-side filtering of malformed WAP Push data SMS, and for recovery, move the physical SIM to a non-Android device so redelivery stops, then clear the corrupted SMS records over ADB.

entries.title: New unpatched PHP RCE (CVE-2026-115560) is separate from PHP2Shell
entries.summary: The PHP security team disclosed a third remote code execution bug, CVE-2026-115560, separate from PHP2Shell, and there is no patch yet. It needs an unusual setup: the app sets session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize, then switches it to php with ini_set() before session_start(). The stopgap is session.upload_progress.enabled=0. BleepingComputer also reports that PHP2Shell exploitation attempts began before disclosure, seen by several vendors including Amazon, and Dataminr reported no confirmed compromises as of Thursday.

lessons.point: The new bug needs a specific runtime handler switch. Check exposure by searching code for ini_set calls on session.serialize_handler made before session_start().
lessons.excerpt: An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().

lessons.point: Disabling session upload progress is the PHP team's stopgap until a patch ships.
lessons.excerpt: Until a security patch is available, the PHP devs suggested setting session.upload_progress.enabled=0

lessons.point: Pre-disclosure PHP2Shell exploitation attempts came from several actors, judging by different payloads and anonymization infrastructure.
lessons.excerpt: The actual payloads and choices in anonymization infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors.

lessons.point: For PHP2Shell, the activity seen since disclosure is scanning and non-working exploits, with no known compromises.
lessons.excerpt: observed activity since vulnerability disclosure remains limited to scanning, fingerprinting, and use of non-working exploits, with no known compromises

entries.takeaway: Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 on any PHP host that might switch session serializers at runtime. It is the stopgap for CVE-2026-115560 until a patch ships.

actionable.title: Check for runtime serialize_handler switching and disable upload progress
actionable.detail: Search PHP code for ini_set('session.serialize_handler', ...) calls made before session_start(), and check php.ini for session.serialize_handler set to php_binary or php_serialize. On any host where you cannot rule this out, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 and keep it until the PHP release that fixes CVE-2026-115560.

entries.prior_art: The pool has the Wiz PHP2Shell disclosure and the Talos PHP2Shell newsletter (CVE-2026-109618/109619). CVE-2026-115560 is a distinct new bug, and the multi-actor pre-disclosure exploitation detail is not in the pool yet.
entries.threat: Remote code execution through PHP's session handling in apps that switch the session serializer at runtime.
entries.conditions: session.serialize_handler set to php_binary or php_serialize in config, switched to php with ini_set() before session_start(), and session upload progress enabled.
entries.mitigations: Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the fixing release ships, avoid switching serialize handlers at runtime, and patch PHP2Shell separately.

entries.title: GitHub previews a package firewall that blocks risky npm installs
entries.summary: GitHub put a package firewall into public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud. It sits between endpoints (including coding agents and CI/CD hosts) or internal registries and the upstream npm registry, and blocks downloads that fail policy. The policies are known-malware advisories, a vulnerability severity threshold (default Critical only), Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) attestation downgrades, newly added preinstall or postinstall scripts, and a minimum package age (default 1 day, range 1 to 365). Rust's Cargo is adding a similar minimum publish age with a 7-day default.

lessons.point: The firewall is a proxy, so it only protects clients that are pointed at it instead of the public registry.
lessons.excerpt: the firewall is placed between endpoints or internal registries and the upstream package repositories

lessons.point: One policy flags versions that newly add install hooks, which targets the common pattern of a hijacked package gaining a malicious postinstall script.
lessons.excerpt: Block newly-introduced install scripts by checking whether the package recently added scripts that run using preinstall or postinstall hooks

lessons.point: The default cooldown is only 1 day, much shorter than the 7-day default Cargo plans, so teams should raise it deliberately.
lessons.excerpt: The value can range from 1 to 365 days. The default value is 1 day.

lessons.point: Socket notes that cooldowns buy detection time, not safety: a malicious release that nobody detects passes once it is old enough.
lessons.excerpt: A release that escapes detection can simply outlast the cooldown.

entries.takeaway: Install-time gating is moving into the platform, but its value depends on routing agents and CI through it and setting a longer cooldown than the 1-day default.

actionable.title: Route agent and CI npm installs through a policy proxy
actionable.detail: Point coding agents and CI runners at a package firewall or internal registry rather than registry.npmjs.org, and block direct egress to the public registry so they cannot bypass it. Turn on the malware, attestation-downgrade and new-install-script policies, and raise minimum package age above the 1-day default (Cargo plans a 7-day default). Keep a fast exception path for urgent security fixes.

entries.verify_note: Verifier upheld lessons; Dependabot's 3-day figure appears only in a link, so it was removed from the text; the cooldown quote is Socket's.
entries.prior_art: Dependency cooldowns are already in the pool (GitHub's 3-day Dependabot cooldown, Semgrep's one-week org-wide cooldown, Chainguard-style interposed scanning), and commercial registry firewalls exist. New here is a GitHub-hosted install-time gate that combines cooldown with attestation-downgrade and newly-added-install-script checks.
entries.threat: Malicious or hijacked npm versions run code when installed, especially when AI agents and CI runners install dependencies automatically.
entries.conditions: GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, npm only, public preview. Clients must be configured to use the firewall.
entries.mitigations: Route installs through the firewall, enable malware, severity, attestation-downgrade and install-script policies, set a multi-day cooldown, and still pin lockfiles and monitor runtime egress because import-time payloads are not caught by install-script checks.

entries.title: KeyDrift malware steals Cisco SD-WAN encryption keys from hacked controllers
entries.summary: Cisco Talos says a group it tracks as UAT-11473 exploited CVE-2026-20127, a CVSS 10.0 authentication bypass in Catalyst SD-WAN (software-defined wide area network) control systems, and planted custom malware called KeyDrift. On a compromised Controller, its LittleFilch component hooks the vdaemon process, reads decrypted control messages and copies the AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard) key material the Controller passes between routers. The main module, PolyFlame, runs in memory, takes commands inside SD-WAN control traffic and has no hardcoded server address.

lessons.point: The implant targets the key-distribution process itself: on a compromised Controller it reads decrypted control messages, where Talos assesses it collects key material for a preset list of edge routers.
lessons.excerpt: On a compromised Controller, a KeyDrift component called LittleFilch hooks into vdaemon and reads control messages after they are decrypted.

lessons.point: Commands arrive inside SD-WAN control traffic and the analyzed samples carried no hardcoded server address, so there is no fixed command server to block.
lessons.excerpt: It is built to accept commands within SD-WAN control traffic, and the analyzed samples contained no hardcoded server address.

lessons.point: Port restrictions do not remove an implant that is already installed, and Talos does not say whether upgrading does, so compromised devices need a separate investigation.
lessons.excerpt: Blocking the ports does not remove malware already on a device.

lessons.point: Detection has to rely on file paths, auth logs and Snort rules, because Talos published no hash, IP address or domain indicators.
lessons.excerpt: Talos's report does not include a list of file hashes, IP addresses or domains for KeyDrift.

entries.takeaway: Patching an SD-WAN control system that was already compromised is not enough: hunt for KeyDrift's files and treat the inter-site keys as possibly exposed.

actionable.title: Hunt for KeyDrift on Catalyst SD-WAN control components
actionable.detail: Upgrade to the first fixed release for your train. Until then, limit ports 22 and 830 to known controller IP addresses. On every Controller, Manager and Validator, check for a modified etc/sv/sshd/run script, /etc/sv/aaamgr/, conf_sshd, rsshd, libdssl.so, libcommon.so, /tmp/system-vdaemon and /var/tmp/vdaemon.bin. Search /var/log/auth.log for 'Accepted publickey for vmanage-admin' from unknown IP addresses. Turn on Snort 2 rules 67387-67416, which ship disabled. If you find signs of compromise, rebuild from patched images and consider rotating the keys.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: facts hold; two lesson points stated inferences as certain (IP blocking, patching), reworded to the source's hedged wording. Novelty lowered to the verifier's 35.
entries.prior_art: Closest are 'Volt Typhoon hides zero-day attacks behind rotating relays of hacked devices' and 'Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator SQL injection (CVE-2026-114625) is exploited in the wild' in product-security. Neither covers an implant that steals keys from the SD-WAN control plane.
entries.threat: An unauthenticated remote attacker uses CVE-2026-20127 to get admin access on Catalyst SD-WAN control systems. They install an in-memory backdoor that copies the AES-256 keys protecting traffic between sites and hides its commands in SD-WAN control traffic.
entries.conditions: Catalyst SD-WAN Controller, Manager or Validator on an unpatched release, on-premises or Cisco-hosted, regardless of configuration. Implants planted before the upgrade may still be present.
entries.mitigations: Upgrade to the first fixed release, since there is no workaround. Restrict ports 22 and 830 to known controller IP addresses. Follow Cisco's hardening guide. Hunt for the listed KeyDrift files and the vmanage-admin publickey logins. Enable the Talos Snort rules. If compromise is found, rebuild control components from patched images and contact Cisco TAC (Technical Assistance Center).

entries.title: Two KSMBD RCE flaws hit public kernel lists with no patch
entries.summary: Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative sent two KSMBD reports (ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549) to public kernel mailing lists without patches. ZDI-CAN-33774 is an unauthenticated race in protocol dispatch on port 445; ZDI-CAN-33549 is an integer underflow in the SMB Direct path needing RDMA. Neither had a mainline fix or a CVE, and the reports credit Trend Micro's AI scanner. The kernel's rules treat AI-found bugs as public, which explains the routing. The primary posts are on lore.kernel.org, which blocks automated fetches, so this cites The Hacker News.

lessons.point: One flaw is reachable before login on any KSMBD server.
lessons.excerpt: ZDI-CAN-33774 requires no authentication, exposing any server running KSMBD on port 445.

lessons.point: An AI scanner was credited with the discovery.
lessons.excerpt: The ZDI reports credit TrendAI, Trend Micro's AI scanner, as the finder.

lessons.point: No fix and no CVE at disclosure time.
lessons.excerpt: neither flaw has a named fix in the mainline kernel

lessons.point: A simple check shows whether you are exposed.
lessons.excerpt: Running systemctl status ksmbd or lsmod | grep ksmbd confirms whether the module is active.

entries.takeaway: If you run KSMBD, check whether it is loaded and limit port 445 exposure until fixes land; AI-found bugs now arrive on public lists.

actionable.title: Find and fence KSMBD
actionable.detail: Run the module check on Linux file servers, unload or firewall KSMBD where unneeded, and track the Linux stable trees for the fixes; consider moving SMB service to Samba until patched.

entries.prior_art: Public disclosure before a patch is unusual; the kernel's policy that AI-found bugs go to public lists is the new process point. Verifier: Prior KSMBD CVEs (CVE-2022-47939, CVE-2023-3866, ZDI-found ksmbd bugs); Linux kernel May 2026 AI-bug-is-public policy and Big Sleep style AI-found kernel bugs
entries.verify_note: Independent verifier found every claim supported by the source.

editorial.reason: Unpatched AI-found kernel RCEs reached public lists; process change worth knowing.

entries.title: Collabora CODE Server for Nextcloud command injection exploited in the wild (CVE-2026-110447)
entries.summary: The Built-in CODE Server app for Nextcloud (richdocumentscode) before 26.4.303 has an OS command injection in proxy.php that gives remote code execution. It triggers when the CODE server is not running, for example right after a restart. It was exploited in September and October 2026, and CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog with a three-day due date; standalone Collabora Online servers are not affected.

lessons.excerpt: The vulnerability is not present in standalone Collabora Online servers; only this deployment with CODE Server is affected.

lessons.point: The injectable path is reachable when the CODE server is not running, such as after a restart.
lessons.excerpt: This is an OS command injection in proxy.php when the CODE server isn't running (e.g., the product was recently restarted).

lessons.point: Exploitation is confirmed, and versions before 26.4.303 are affected.
lessons.excerpt: allows remote code execution, as exploited in the wild in September and October 2026

entries.takeaway: Nextcloud instances using the built-in CODE server need richdocumentscode 26.4.303 or later now, plus a check for signs of compromise.

actionable.title: Update richdocumentscode and hunt for proxy.php abuse
actionable.detail: Inventory Nextcloud servers with the Collabora Built-in CODE Server app (richdocumentscode) and upgrade to 26.4.303+. Review web logs for unusual requests to richdocumentscode proxy.php, especially around restarts, and check for unexpected child processes of the PHP/web server user. Verifier: Standard KEV-listed unauthenticated OS command injection in a self-hosted collaboration add-on; closest prior is the earlier richdocumentscode/Collabora CVE-2025-66208 that NVD explicitly distinguishes; no prior entry in the tracker data.

entries.title: InfraTrust report says network appliances wait on vendors for PHP2Shell fixes
entries.summary: Eclypsium's October InfraTrust Pulse tracked 133 advisories from 18 vendors covering 2,813 vulnerabilities. Sixteen of those advisories include flaws already being exploited, and the report highlights exploited flaws in Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, FortiMail and PAN-OS. Many firewalls, VPNs and storage appliances build PHP into their management interfaces. Customers cannot apply the PHP2Shell fixes (CVE-2026-109618/109619) themselves and must wait for vendor firmware.

lessons.point: PHP compiled into appliance firmware means the fix depends on each vendor, not the customer.
lessons.excerpt: Because vendors compile PHP into appliance firmware, customers commonly cannot install the recent PHP security updates themselves and must instead wait for each vendor to release updated firmware.

lessons.point: Until firmware arrives, take PHP-backed management interfaces off the internet.
lessons.excerpt: InfraTrust therefore recommends that administrators make sure PHP-backed management interfaces are not exposed to the Internet while waiting for PHP2Shell patches.

lessons.point: Bundled components keep spreading flaws across vendors. The Copy Fail Linux kernel bug keeps showing up in more advisories.
lessons.excerpt: has now appeared in 29 advisories across eight vendors, up from 19 advisories from six vendors last month.

entries.takeaway: On appliances, patch speed depends on the vendor's firmware schedule, so limit exposure of management interfaces now instead of waiting.

actionable.title: Pull PHP-backed appliance management interfaces off the internet
actionable.detail: List firewalls, VPN gateways, application delivery controllers and network-attached storage whose web management interface uses PHP (Palo Alto, F5, NetScaler, Check Point and QNAP have confirmed affected products). Block internet access to those interfaces until vendor firmware with patched PHP ships. Patch NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure first.

entries.prior_art: Many PHP2Shell entries in product-security.json ('PHP2Shell hits every PHP since 5.4', 'Patch PHP and inventory PHP runtimes', AWS-logged exploitation). New: appliances with PHP built into firmware depend on vendor rebuilds.
entries.threat: Attackers exploit edge and management appliances, including through PHP2Shell unauthenticated RCE in PHP-based management interfaces, to get initial access to corporate networks.
entries.conditions: Appliances with PHP built into their firmware management interface that are reachable from the internet, or unpatched NetScaler, Ivanti, Check Point, Cisco, Arista, FortiMail, F5 or PAN-OS products listed in the report.
entries.mitigations: Do not expose PHP-backed management interfaces to the internet until vendor firmware arrives, and prioritize the NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure patches, then Fortinet's October 22 updates.

editorial.reason: PHP2Shell is the theme of the week. This adds a lesson that changes what defenders do: appliances with PHP compiled into their firmware cannot be patched by customers, so pull their management interfaces off the internet now.

entries.title: Hijacked coding assistant recommended a PyPI package that stole GitHub tokens
entries.summary: SafeDep summarizes a reported incident. An attacker took control of a developer's live AI coding assistant session and had it recommend a PyPI package hiding an infostealer. The stolen high-privilege GitHub OAuth tokens let the Shai-Hulud worm copy itself into about 100 internal repos and plant a poisoned package in the internal namespace. The cited report lists three ways attackers take over assistants: prompt injection (which also fooled LLM-based security scanners), tampered startup hooks, and backdoored agent skills. The post does not explain how the session in the main incident was hijacked.

lessons.point: The entry point was the assistant's suggestion, not the registry or the CI pipeline. Whoever controls what the assistant recommends controls what gets installed.
lessons.excerpt: The attacker got control of an active AI coding assistant session belonging to a developer.

lessons.point: LLM-based security scanners can be prompt-injected by the same payload they are meant to catch, so they cannot be the only gate.
lessons.excerpt: They also targeted the language model based security scanners intended to detect such attempts.

lessons.point: Repository-level assistant hooks run code as soon as you open the project, with no suggestion to accept or prompt to approve.
lessons.excerpt: In another case, attackers modified the command line hooks an assistant runs on startup.

lessons.point: Shai-Hulud now hunts credentials in AI tool settings files, which often hold plaintext keys.
lessons.excerpt: A newer variant searches 469 locations for credentials, up from 189.

lessons.point: Teams scan the lockfile but not the assistant that picked what went into it.
lessons.excerpt: Most teams scan their lockfiles and their pull requests, and almost nobody scans the thing that decided what went into the lockfile in the first place.

entries.takeaway: Treat any package your coding assistant suggests as untrusted input. Check it against an allowlist and hashes in CI, and keep long-lived GitHub tokens and AI tool config secrets off developer machines.

actionable.title: Gate assistant-suggested dependencies and sweep AI tool configs for secrets
actionable.detail: Route all installs through an internal proxy with an approved-package list. In CI, fail any new lockfile entry that is not on the list or whose hash does not match the registry. Search AI tool config directories (for example ~/.claude, ~/.cursor, ~/.codeium, ~/.config) for plaintext tokens and rotate any you find. Replace long-lived GitHub OAuth and personal access tokens with short-lived OIDC-based ones. Review repository hook configs (for example .claude/settings.json hooks) in pull requests like code.

entries.prior_art: 'Mini Shai-Hulud still spreads four months on via never-restored hijacked actions-cool/issues-helper tags, planting Claude Code and VS Code hooks in six repos' and 'keyv/cacheable Mini Shai-Hulud' (product-security corpus / archive); OpenClaw ClawHub skill marketplace entries. New here is the assistant session as the first step, but the source gives no detail on how it was hijacked. Verifier's closest: Mini Shai-Hulud Claude Code/VS Code hook entries; OpenClaw ClawHub malicious skills.
entries.verify_note: Verifier: facts match; secondhand sourcing (incident attributed to unnamed researchers, report cited only for takeover routes).
entries.threat: An attacker who controls an AI coding assistant session, through prompt injection, tampered hooks or a malicious skill, steers it to recommend a malicious package. The stolen developer tokens then let a worm spread through internal repos and the internal package namespace.
entries.conditions: Developers accept assistant-suggested dependencies without review; high-privilege long-lived GitHub OAuth tokens sit on developer machines; the internal namespace is writable with those tokens; AI tool configs hold plaintext secrets.
entries.mitigations: Allowlist and hash checks for dependencies in CI; an internal registry proxy; short-lived OIDC credentials; keep tokens away from editor extensions; review agent skills, hooks and MCP servers like dependencies; do not rely on LLM scanners alone.

entries.title: A Lean 4 string-slice mismatch let native_decide 'prove' Fermat's Last Theorem
entries.summary: Trail of Bits, while experimenting with a code-review skill using GPT-5.6, found that Lean's String.Pos.Raw.extract returns the empty string in its logical definition but the whole original string in compiled native code for an astronomically large position. Combining the two evaluations yields a contradiction, so any theorem, including Fermat's Last Theorem, can be 'proved' using native_decide. The Lean team fixed the memory-safety part within about three hours and the semantic mismatch five days after the report. The authors say it is not a kernel soundness issue.

lessons.point: A disagreement between a prover's logical definition and its compiled implementation is enough to derive a contradiction.
lessons.excerpt: That disagreement is enough to manufacture a contradiction.

lessons.point: native_decide puts the compiler inside the trusted boundary, so check axioms when validating external proofs.
lessons.excerpt: The extra axiom `native_decide` adds the compiler to the trusted boundary, and therefore needs to be used with care.

lessons.point: The bug sits in a low-level string-slicing primitive, not the kernel.
lessons.excerpt: The issue affects `String.Pos.Raw.extract`, Lean’s low-level string-slicing function.

lessons.point: The upstream response was fast.
lessons.excerpt: About 90 minutes after we reported the issue, hargoniX opened a fix for the

entries.takeaway: Machine-checked proofs are only as trustworthy as the evaluators behind them, so audit the axioms (especially native_decide) and prefer independent checkers for high-stakes results.

actionable.title: Audit axioms when accepting external Lean proofs
actionable.detail: Upgrade to Lean v4.34.0-rc1 or later (affected: stable versions up to 4.33.1), run #print axioms on external proofs and treat any dependence on native_decide as adding the compiler to the trusted base; consider independent checkers such as lean4lean for high-stakes proofs.

entries.prior_art: none found in pool. Verifier: none equivalent found (no Lean/proof-assistant entries in the data files)
entries.verify_note: All claims and excerpts verified (3-hour memory-safety fix, 5-day semantic fix, 4.33.1 affected). Genuine, novel logical-vs-native disagreement bug, but narrow audience for appsec engineers.

entries.title: CISA KEV: exploited Fortinet CVE-2025-61624 lets read-write admins write or delete files
entries.summary: CISA added CVE-2025-61624 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on October 16, 2026, with a remediation due date of October 19. lessons.excerpt: may allow an authenticated attacker with admin profile and at least read-write permissions to write or delete arbitrary files via specific CLI commands

lessons.point: CISA added it to the KEV catalog on October 16 with a remediation deadline three days later.
lessons.excerpt: October 16, 2026 | October 19, 2026

actionable.detail: Inventory FortiOS, FortiProxy, FortiPAM and FortiSwitchManager (and Siemens RUGGEDCOM APE1808) devices and upgrade each to the fixed release for its train per Fortinet advisory FG-IR-26-122. entries.title: A few notes on AWS Nitro Enclaves: KMS integration
entries.summary: Trail of Bits enumerates passive and active attack classes against the Nitro Enclave to AWS KMS communication channel: encryption-context omission, CMK substitution, attestation-request replay, and the fact that TLS to KMS terminates outside the HSM. They also flag an end-to-end verifiability gap: even with immutable key policies, AWS Support can restore default policies for a key owner, so there is no Certificate-Transparency-style public log a third-party client can independently verify.
entries.takeaway: Enclave-to-KMS attestation only closes the gap if you also hardcode the CMK ARN, attest the IAM role, and initiate TLS from inside the enclave; without that, active-attacker equivalence returns.

lessons.point: Attestation documents are not cryptographically bound to KMS requests, so a captured attestation is replayable for five minutes against any supported operation with attacker-chosen parameters.
lessons.excerpt: As attestations are not cryptographically bound to the requests, the attacker can use the attestation with any supported operation with arbitrary params.

lessons.point: KMS terminates TLS outside the HSM, so end-to-end confidentiality between the enclave and the HSM is not achievable and AWS insiders belong in the threat model.
lessons.excerpt: KMS terminates TLS outside of HSM ([most likely](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/cryptographic-details/internal-communication-security.html)), and the attestation's pubkey encryption is probably done outside of HSM. This makes it impossible to have an end-to-end TLS channel between enclave and HSM, and AWS insiders may theoretically constitute an active attacker threat.

lessons.point: Even immutable key policies do not deliver true end-to-end verifiability, because AWS Support can restore a default policy on the owner's request and there is no public append-only log a third party can audit.
lessons.excerpt: Note that key owners can always [contact AWS support to restore default key policies]... However, we are not aware of any "Certificate Transparency"-style public, append-only log for KMS key policies that an external party can independently verify.

lessons.point: The official aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c is C code that Trail of Bits found host-exploitable and recommends avoiding in favor of a Rust NSM library plus Boto3 for KMS.
lessons.excerpt: Amazon ships a lot of SDKs for various tasks. Among them is [`aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c`](https://github.com/aws/aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c) that provides tools and a library for enclaves-KMS communication. Avoid it: this particular SDK is written in C, and we found it contains vulnerabilities that can be used to exploit enclaves from the parent host.

actionable.title: Enclave-KMS hardening checklist
actionable.detail: For any enclave-KMS integration: hardcode CMK ARN (attested), attest the IAM role via sts:GetCallerIdentity, initiate TLS from inside the enclave with a pinned Amazon CA, use encryption contexts that the host cannot fully control, and monitor kms:PutKeyPolicy externally since AWS Support can restore default policies.

entries.prior_art: No direct pool entry; the Trail of Bits Nitro Enclaves attack-surface post is cited in this piece but not indexed. Standing claims do not cover KMS-enclave attestation replay.
entries.threat: A privileged host or malicious insider between enclave and KMS can swap ciphertexts, substitute CMKs, replay attestations, or bypass immutable key policies via AWS Support restoration.
entries.conditions: Applies when a Nitro Enclave uses KMS with attestation-based key access, does not initiate its own TLS to KMS, or uses key aliases instead of full CMK ARNs.
entries.mitigations: Bundle KMS CA cert inside the enclave and pin it; initiate TLS from within the enclave; attest full CMK ARN and IAM role; use encryption contexts under enclave control; deny kms:PutKeyPolicy globally; alarm on key deletion; publish a client-visible policy monitor. Prefer aws-nitro-enclaves-nsm-api (Rust) + Boto3 over aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c (C).
entries.verify_note: All four excerpts verified verbatim against raw_path. Cluster set to null because the piece is enclave-crypto/appsec and does not intersect the 13 clusters (nearest fit I is 'Deployment infra and sandboxing', but the material is HSM/KMS cryptography, not agent/LLM runtime).

entries.title: A compromised DebugBear monitoring script drained Polymarket traders' accounts
entries.summary: Polymarket halted trading on October 29 after malicious JavaScript, served from website performance monitoring firm DebugBear's RUM (real user monitoring) script, hijacked logged-in sessions. The code found each user's trading tools and either sold positions and moved the proceeds or sent position tokens to an attacker address. Hudson Rock found no routine that sent credentials or keys anywhere: the script simply reused the authority of the logged-in session. Loss estimates range from about $2.19 million to $2.71 million.

lessons.point: A third-party script running in an authenticated page needs no stolen credentials, because it can act with the logged-in user's session directly.
lessons.excerpt: Its central approach is to reuse authority already available in the authenticated application

lessons.point: The payload was written for this specific app and adapted to the account type to move funds.
lessons.excerpt: Depending on the account type, it then tried either to sell positions and move the proceeds, or to send position tokens straight to an attacker-set address.

lessons.point: The vendor's fix was to remove the snippet, which shows how much power an embedded monitoring tag has.
lessons.excerpt: urged users of its real user monitoring (RUM) product to pull its snippet from their websites

lessons.point: This is Polymarket's second frontend third-party script compromise this year, which suggests a structural exposure.
lessons.excerpt: another third-party compromise that injected a malicious script into its frontend, with losses reported at around $3 million

entries.takeaway: Do not load third-party monitoring or analytics scripts into authenticated pages that can move money: anything in that page can act as the user.

actionable.title: Isolate third-party scripts from transactional pages
actionable.detail: List every third-party script loaded on authenticated pages. Remove monitoring and analytics tags from pages that can trade, withdraw or transfer, or self-host pinned copies with Subresource Integrity hashes and a strict CSP (Content Security Policy) script-src. Require step-up confirmation for fund movements so a script running in the page cannot complete them silently.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: all four lessons supported; loss figures are press estimates.
entries.prior_art: Closest is 'Skimmers hijacked Convertr's self-hosted analytics script to steal checkout card data' in product-security, the same compromised-shared-script pattern. Here the script performed in-session financial actions rather than skimming data.
entries.threat: An attacker tampers with a vendor's hosted monitoring script. The script runs inside users' authenticated sessions on a trading site, and sells positions or transfers tokens to an attacker-controlled address.
entries.conditions: A site loads a third-party script, here DebugBear's RUM snippet, from vendor-controlled infrastructure into pages where logged-in users can move funds.
entries.mitigations: Remove the compromised snippet. Keep third-party scripts off transactional pages, or self-host them with Subresource Integrity and a strict Content Security Policy. Require explicit user confirmation for fund movements.

entries.title: A probability-scoring model matches employee accounts to one person at 0.95 F1
entries.summary: Vincenzo Iozzo ran a three-step pipeline (exact email, a 20-candidate Jaro-Winkler shortlist, then a model decision) across five real environments. TypeSafe's Jev model answers yes/no with a probability. It reached 0.948 F1 on four large orgs against 0.894 for Haiku 4.5 and 0.911 for Sonnet 5, at $0.62 per 1,000 accounts and 0.3 s median latency. A gpt-oss-20b baseline gated at 95% merged look-alike service accounts across different AWS accounts, and classic record linkage fell to 0.70 F1 on a small messy directory.
entries.takeaway: In identity governance (IGA) and identity-security products, a cheap probability model with a tuned cut-off, plus a frontier-model check only on the 'maybe' band, beats rules and a fixed-confidence LLM gate, but validate on your own data first.

lessons.point: Traditional record linkage holds up on clean, large directories but breaks on messy ones. That messy tail is where LLM-style judgment pays off.
lessons.excerpt: Classic record linkage came close on large, regular directories (F1 0.91 vs 0.95) but collapsed on a small, messy one (0.70 vs 0.92).

lessons.point: A fixed 95% confidence gate copied from another model throws away most true matches for an underconfident model. Pick the threshold per model.
lessons.excerpt: With the baseline’s 95% gate, Jev rejects most real matches. At its natural cut-off of 0.5 it is excellent.

lessons.point: The cheaper Claude models over-link: they merge different people who share a first name and similar service accounts, even when the prompt explicitly forbids those patterns.
lessons.excerpt: The smaller models follow those negative rules less reliably than a model trained specifically to answer yes/no questions like this one.

lessons.point: Sending only the 'maybe' band to a second model lifted F1 on the messy Org D environment from 0.65 to 0.86, but cost a little precision elsewhere. The author simulated it from recorded answers, and the judge was also a Claude model, so the result may flatter the hybrid.
lessons.excerpt: So the second opinion is worth turning on where a directory is known to be messy, not everywhere.

actionable.title: Cascade for linking accounts to identities
actionable.detail: 1) Group accounts that share an exact email without AI. 2) Build a top-20 shortlist per account by weighted Jaro-Winkler over names, usernames and emails. 3) Score each candidate pair with a cheap model that returns a probability. Pick the cut-off on a manually linked sample, not a fixed 95%. 4) Send only accounts with a candidate scoring 0.2-0.5 to a stronger model for a second opinion. 5) Merge accepted links with union-find. 6) Decide up front whether plus-addressed test logins and personal guest accounts count as the same person, and spot-check service-account merges across cloud accounts.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: every number and lesson matches the source. Verifier novelty 35 (closest: Red Hat's Jev-style decision-model guardrail benchmark), relevance 40; took the lower novelty.
entries.prior_art: Decades of record-linkage and entity-resolution work. No identity-resolution entry found in the pool. The nearest pool item is DecisionPivot (ai-research), on decision models for routers and guardrails. What's new is a practitioner benchmark on private real directories (low contamination risk) with cost, latency and per-environment error analysis, and the finding that a hybrid helps only on messy data. It is a single-author black-box test with a model judge, so the evidence is moderate.
entries.threat: Wrong identity merges, such as service accounts from different AWS accounts or two people sharing a first name, corrupt the identity graph that access reviews and detections rely on. Missed links leave guest and on-premises accounts unattributed to their owner.
entries.conditions: No federation between systems, so accounts must be linked by naming conventions. The data is messy: duplicate B2B guest invites, numbered sibling accounts, shared test mailboxes. The pipeline uses a fixed confidence gate or a cheap prompted LLM that ignores negative rules.
entries.mitigations: Tune each model's threshold on a manually linked sample, route only uncertain pairs to a stronger model, and review merges that involve service or shared accounts before they feed access decisions.

entries.title: GitLab patches CVE-2026-110264, a CVSS 10.0 unauthenticated RCE in the regex compiler

lessons.point: Affected versions run back to 7.0; fixed releases span seven release lines.
lessons.excerpt: all versions from 7.0 before 18.11.13, 19.0 before 19.0.10

lessons.point: Detections exist for self-managed instances: a native worker crash and a render error burst.
lessons.excerpt: GitLab security has released two threat detections to support customers with self-managed instances

lessons.excerpt: GitLab-managed infrastructure, including GitLab.com and GitLab Dedicated, remains patched.

entries.title: VibeRaven statically checks AI-built Supabase apps for row-level security gaps
entries.summary: VibeRaven is a local command-line tool and MCP server that reads a Vercel and Supabase repository's migrations, code and env files. It flags tables without row level security (RLS), 'using (true)' policies, service_role keys in browser code, security definer functions callable with the anon key, and Stripe webhooks that never check signatures. Its authors scanned 512 public Lovable apps and found that 47.3% exposed at least one security definer function to signed-out callers. It is a repository check only and cannot see policy changes made in the live database dashboard.

lessons.point: AI app builders often expose security definer functions to the anon key. In the authors' static scan of 512 public Lovable repos, nearly half had at least one.
lessons.excerpt: 47.3% (242) define at least one security definer function in the public schema that a signed-out caller with the anon key can run at /rest/v1/rpc

lessons.point: A service_role key shipped to the browser bypasses every RLS policy. A single bundled file can undo all of the database's access control.
lessons.excerpt: This file ships to the browser, and the service role key skips RLS entirely.

lessons.point: Static migration scanning has a blind spot: policies changed in the Supabase dashboard never show up in the repository.
lessons.excerpt: VibeRaven is a repository check, not a live database test. It reads migrations, so it cannot see a policy someone added in the Supabase dashboard.

lessons.point: The README says Lovable and Bolt push straight to main, so a gate that runs only on pull requests would miss those changes.
lessons.excerpt: Lovable and Bolt push straight to `main`, so a pull request check alone misses most of their changes.

entries.takeaway: For AI-built Supabase apps, the common gaps are database authorization mistakes such as missing row-level security (RLS), anon-callable definer functions and leaked service_role keys, and static repository checks catch many of them before launch but you still need a live check of the deployed database.

actionable.title: Run VibeRaven on Supabase app repos on both push and pull request
actionable.detail: Run 'npx -y viberaven@1.6.12 check' in CI, set fail-on-blockers, and trigger it on push to main as well as on pull requests. Add 'revoke execute ... from public, anon, authenticated' for security definer functions in public. Pair it with Supabase Security Advisor and a Playwright test where user A tries to read user B's rows, to cover live-database drift.

entries.verify_note: Verifier rated novelty 12 vs 45: the RLS, service_role and dashboard-blind-spot points are standard Supabase docs and Security Advisor lints; only the vendor's 512-repo statistic is new, and the push-to-main point is an unsupported README assertion.
entries.prior_art: The pool has no Supabase, RLS or vibe-coded-app scanner entry. The nearest is the general ps.ai-code material on gating agent pull requests with automated checks. The 512-repo statistic is the vendor's own and is not independently checked here.
entries.threat: AI-built Vercel and Supabase apps ship tables without RLS, permissive 'using (true)' policies, service_role keys in browser bundles, or security definer functions the anon key can call. Any visitor can then read or change data, or call privileged functions at /rest/v1/rpc.
entries.conditions: An app built with Lovable, Bolt, Cursor or a similar tool uses Supabase's Data API with migrations that do not enable RLS, do not revoke EXECUTE from anon, or that put service keys in client-side code.
entries.mitigations: Enable RLS on every public table. Replace 'using (true)' policies. Keep the service_role key server-side and rotate it if it was exposed. Revoke EXECUTE on security definer functions from public, anon and authenticated. Verify Stripe webhook signatures over the raw body. Check the live project with Supabase Security Advisor.

entries.title: Snyk: SAST cannot see missing ownership checks in agent-written endpoints
entries.summary: Snyk argues that coding agents produce endpoints that check login but not ownership, letting any authenticated user read another tenant's records by changing an ID. The required rule (for example, invoices belong to organizations) lives in the product's data model, not in the file, so neither the agent nor pattern-based SAST can see it. It recommends writing down ownership rules, asking about authorization explicitly on agent PRs, and adding one cross-tenant test per resource type; the post offers no measured data and promotes Snyk's own product.

lessons.point: The failure mode is code that looks correct and passes review while enforcing the wrong policy.
lessons.excerpt: AI coding agents produce authorization logic that compiles, passes review, and enforces the wrong policy.

lessons.point: The agent lacks the product rule that makes the ownership check necessary.
lessons.excerpt: An agent working from the prompt and the surrounding file has no access to the thing that makes the check necessary.

lessons.point: Object-level authorization bugs (CWE-639/862/863) have no source-to-sink shape for SAST rules to match.
lessons.excerpt: The defect is the absence of a comparison that only the application's own rules require.

lessons.point: Fold the ownership condition into the lookup so foreign objects return 404, avoiding ID enumeration via 403.
lessons.excerpt: That is the behavior you want, because a 403 would confirm that the record exists and allow an attacker to enumerate valid identifiers.

lessons.point: A cheap durable control is one cross-tenant test per resource type.
lessons.excerpt: One test per resource, asserting that a valid session from one tenant gets a 404 on another tenant's object, turns the rule you wrote down in step two into one that stays enforced.

entries.takeaway: Agent-written endpoints need an explicit ownership question in review and a cross-tenant test per resource, because neither the agent nor SAST knows your tenancy rules.

actionable.title: Cross-tenant test per resource for agent-authored endpoints
actionable.detail: Inventory routes that take an ID, filename or key from the URL or body. Document each resource's owner field and who may read or modify it. Add a required PR checklist item for agent-authored PRs: 'which field verifies the caller owns this object?' Add one integration test per resource asserting that a valid session from tenant A gets 404 on tenant B's object. Feed the written ownership rules into the agent's context so it can apply them.

entries.prior_art: Archive: 'OWASP Top 10:2025 - Broken Access Control (#1)', 'Rule-Based Dataflow + LLM Reasoning Beats Pure-LLM Scanners 4-5x on Recall for Authorization Bugs', and 'Auditing a cyber benchmark for groundedness: models reason, but 70% of real IDORs are missed by everyone'. This post restates the SAST limit for authorization bugs and applies it to agent-written code without new data. Verifier's closest: OWASP Top 10:2025 Broken Access Control; rule-based dataflow + LLM authz-bug entry.
entries.verify_note: Verifier: supported; vendor post restating the SAST blind spot for object-level authorization, no agent-specific data.
entries.threat: Authenticated users read or modify other tenants' data through agent-written endpoints that lack ownership checks.
entries.conditions: Multi-tenant apps where coding agents generate endpoints from prompts lacking ownership rules; review and SAST as the only gates.
entries.mitigations: Documented ownership rules in agent context; explicit authorization review item on agent PRs; per-resource cross-tenant tests returning 404; context-aware analysis beyond pattern SAST.

entries.title: PHP says Chainguard broke the PHP2Shell embargo with patched images
entries.summary: Rumored CVE IDs led PHP to move its release up one day, and Calif, one of the firms that found the bugs, mistakenly published a proof-of-concept video. PHP says Chainguard, which held the patch early as a distributor, published fixed images to everyone at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release. Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc says other vendors were already seeing real-world exploitation. He also says his team found the same memory-corruption bugs with its AI harness and a frontier model, the night it heard 'something was coming in PHP'.

lessons.point: PHP's point: patched binaries shipped during an embargo act as disclosure, because attackers can study the fix before other users can update.
lessons.excerpt: Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release.

lessons.point: Lorenc's account: a hint that a bug exists in a named project was enough for an AI harness to rediscover it. If that holds more widely, embargoes will hold for less time.
lessons.excerpt: the CEO and the Chainguard team independently found the same memory corruption vulnerabilities.

lessons.point: Moving a release earlier is limited by downstream packagers. PHP chose a one-day shift so distributors could have updates ready at disclosure.
lessons.excerpt: Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update

lessons.point: On Apache with mod_php, one of the bugs triggers before any application code runs, so patch the PHP runtime on those hosts first.
lessons.excerpt: On Apache with mod_php, an unauthenticated request can trigger this before any application code runs.

entries.takeaway: Embargoes now leak through rumors, proof-of-concept videos and early binaries, and an AI harness may turn a hint into a working find within hours, so plan patch rollout for early disclosure.

actionable.title: Write an embargo-break playbook for critical runtime CVEs
actionable.detail: Agree in advance on what justifies shipping a fix before an embargo ends, such as confirmed exploitation or a public proof of concept, and how to notify the coordinator first. Pre-stage patched base images, for example PHP containers, so you can roll them out within hours of a leak. Assume a rumored CVE ID may be enough for attackers to rediscover the bug with AI.

entries.prior_art: The pool has Wiz's PHP2Shell technical write-up and OpenAI's coordinated-disclosure framework for the same CVEs, plus Chainguard's Athena disclosure program in the archive. New here are the distributor-side embargo break, its timeline, and the CEO's claim of AI rediscovery from a hint alone.
entries.threat: Attackers diff patched binaries released early, or rediscover critical bugs with AI from rumors, and exploit them before the coordinated release.
entries.conditions: A critical bug in widely deployed software, many downstream distributors holding pre-release patches, and rumors or partial details circulating before release.
entries.mitigations: Distributors follow the coordinator's timeline unless an agreed exploitation trigger is met, and notify the coordinator before shipping. Maintainers plan for shorter embargoes. Operators patch the PHP runtime immediately, including container images.
entries.verify_note: Two independent verifier passes (draft and final text): all excerpts verbatim, attribution of PHP's view vs Lorenc's correct (not refuted). Novelty: lowest of 42, 30 and 66.

editorial.reason: The PHP2Shell embargo dispute shows how disclosure now breaks down (rumors, PoC video, early distributor binaries, AI rediscovery from a hint); a transferable lesson for patch planning.

entries.title: Exploited Linux kernel flaw lets IPsec decryption overwrite page-cache data
entries.summary: CISA added CVE-2026-46300 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on 2026-10-28. Per CISA's description, a missing variable initialization in the Linux kernel loses the shared-fragment marker when socket buffers are coalesced, so Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP, the IPsec encryption protocol) input processing decrypts shared fragments in place and can modify page-cache-backed data. The fetched NVD page holds only references: oss-security mailing list posts from May 2026 and a long run of Red Hat errata; it gives no affected versions or exploitation details.

lessons.point: The bug was discussed publicly on the oss-security mailing list in May 2026, months before CISA's October KEV listing.
lessons.excerpt: http://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/05/13/5

lessons.point: Red Hat has shipped many kernel errata for this CVE, so distribution kernel updates are the fix path.
lessons.excerpt: https://access.redhat.com/errata/RHSA-2026:19521

entries.takeaway: A kernel bug disclosed in May is now exploited in the wild, so any Linux host still on an unpatched kernel needs the vendor update now.

actionable.title: Patch and reboot Linux kernels for CVE-2026-46300
actionable.detail: Check your distribution's advisory for CVE-2026-46300 (Red Hat has published errata), install the fixed kernel, and reboot so it is running. Put hosts that terminate IPsec traffic first, and track the KEV due date.

entries.verify_note: Lessons upheld from the NVD reference list; the bug mechanism in the summary comes from the CISA KEV record, not the NVD page.
entries.prior_art: No entry for this CVE in the pool. Page-cache corruption through kernel bugs is a known class (for example Dirty Pipe, CVE-2022-0847). The new facts are this specific ESP coalescing bug and CISA's confirmation that it is exploited.
entries.threat: Per CISA's description, exploitation can modify page-cache-backed data through IPsec ESP input processing. The NVD page gives no exploitation details.

entries.title: Check Point: fake ChatGPT and Claude apps sideload malware via signed installers
entries.summary: Check Point Research tracked a campaign it calls Yoba that used GitHub repositories and GitHub.io pages posing as desktop apps named GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus, which rank on Google through search poisoning. Their downloads pair a legitimate signed OpenAI or Anthropic `Setup.exe` with a malicious `winmm.dll` that the installer loads, and the malware persists through a scheduled task that loads a second library through the Windows Media Player binary `WMPDMC.exe`. The loader finds its server by reading a Telegram channel's profile image and using its last 50 bytes to seed a word-list domain generator.

lessons.point: A trusted signed vendor binary is the carrier; the malicious code is the library placed beside it.
lessons.excerpt: `Setup.exe`, a legitimate signed OpenAI executable, is used during execution to sideload the malicious DLL.

lessons.point: The lure ranks on Google rather than GitHub search, so no fake stars were needed.
lessons.excerpt: they still appear among the top results on Google. This is most likely due to SEO poisoning

lessons.point: The server address hides in a Telegram profile picture, so changing the picture moves the server.
lessons.excerpt: By changing the image of the Telegram channel, a new domain can be generated.

lessons.point: The archives were not password-protected because anti-analysis checks already kept detection low.
lessons.excerpt: neither of these repositories used password protection, as the binaries already had very low detection rates thanks to their anti-sandbox and other anti-analysis techniques.

entries.takeaway: People searching for desktop AI apps are a live lure, so allow AI clients only from vendor sites and alert when signed vendor installers load libraries from download folders.

actionable.title: Hunt for Yoba's sideloading and persistence artifacts
actionable.detail: Search endpoints for a ProgramData\WMProcess folder holding WMPDMC.exe and wmpdui.dll, scheduled tasks described as "Collects device metadata for Windows Media Player." that run as Local System, and winmm.dll next to a signed OpenAI or Anthropic Setup.exe. Block AI desktop app downloads from GitHub releases and GitHub.io pages by policy.

entries.prior_art: Fake AI-tool installers and loading malicious libraries through signed binaries are established techniques; seeding a domain generator from a Telegram channel's profile image is the less common detail.
entries.threat: Windows malware delivered as fake ChatGPT and Claude desktop apps, persisting with Local System rights.
entries.conditions: A user downloads an AI desktop app from a search result that leads to a GitHub repository or GitHub.io page and runs it as administrator.
entries.mitigations: Allow AI clients only from vendor domains, block execution from download folders, and hunt for the WMProcess folder and the Windows Media Player scheduled task.

entries.title: A client's 1-bit reply leaks the full CKKS secret key
entries.source_name: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (via arXiv)
entries.summary: CKKS is a homomorphic encryption scheme that lets a server compute on encrypted data. The attack targets deployments that publish coefficient-to-slot (C2S) evaluation keys and in which the client reveals whether a returned ciphertext was valid. The malicious evaluator builds ciphertexts whose validity depends on whether one secret-key coefficient matches a guess, and recovers a ternary key in O(H) queries, where H is the key's entropy. The attack does not break the underlying lattice problem (RLWE) or CKKS's chosen-plaintext security (IND-CPA); it fully recovered keys for four standard CKKS presets in Lattigo v6.2.0.
entries.takeaway: If you deploy homomorphic encryption with an untrusted server, any client behaviour the server can observe on decryption, such as errors, retries or a 1-bit validity signal, is a key-recovery oracle, even though the scheme itself is secure.

lessons.point: This is a protocol and deployment flaw, not a cryptographic break. Sound primitives still leak through the client's observable reactions.
lessons.excerpt: The attack does not break RLWE or CKKS IND-CPA security.

lessons.point: The attack is practical: full key recovery on four standard parameter presets in Lattigo v6.2.0.
lessons.excerpt: We implemented the full end-to-end attack in Lattigo v6.2.0 and recovered the full secret key across four parameter sets drawn from standard CKKS presets.

lessons.point: Each query is re-randomized, so it evades trivial client-side detection of repeated malicious ciphertexts.
lessons.excerpt: each submitted query is independently randomized with a fresh encryption of zero

actionable.title: Remove the validity oracle from CKKS client protocols
actionable.detail: Review homomorphic encryption deployments where the evaluator is not fully trusted and C2S/bootstrapping keys are public. Make sure the client does not expose decryption validity (error messages, retries, timing, aborts) back to the evaluator. Rotate keys after any suspected exposure, and treat a malicious-evaluator threat model as distinct from the scheme's IND-CPA guarantee.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: core facts match; flagged 'widely used library' and 'does not work' as overstated (both fixed). Verifier novelty 55 (closest: Li-Micciancio IND-CPA-D CKKS attacks), relevance 35.
entries.prior_art: The pool has only 'Making private AI practical with homomorphic encryption (HEIR)' in the archive, which covers the tooling, not attacks. The general class of reaction and decryption-failure attacks on lattice schemes and earlier CKKS key-recovery work exists outside the pool. The delta is an asymptotically optimal query count through public C2S keys plus a working attack on Lattigo. This is niche for most product-security readers.
entries.threat: A malicious homomorphic evaluator, such as a cloud server, recovers the client's ternary CKKS secret key and can then decrypt all of the client's data.
entries.conditions: A CKKS deployment that publishes coefficient-to-slot evaluation keys (as bootstrapping does), where the client returns a 1-bit validity response or equivalent observable reaction for ciphertexts the evaluator submits.
entries.mitigations: Design the client so the evaluator cannot observe decryption validity, and do not rely on CKKS IND-CPA security alone when the evaluator may be malicious.

entries.title: CVM-Store paper protects confidential VM storage at near-raw disk speed
entries.summary: Confidential virtual machines encrypt memory in use but leave persistent storage outside their trust boundary, exposed to the cloud provider. CVM-Store, accepted at the NDSS 2027 conference, combines authenticated encryption with a userspace input/output engine to give confidentiality, integrity and freshness, and uses a trusted counter service for rollback protection. It reports staying within about 1% of raw disk bandwidth for writes and 1-19% for reads of large objects; only the abstract was available.

lessons.point: Confidential VMs protect memory, not disks, so stored data stays exposed to the provider.
lessons.excerpt: they protect only data in use; persistent storage lies outside the CVM trust boundary, exposing all stateful data to the cloud provider.

lessons.point: The overhead comes from combining encryption and input/output naively, not from either alone.
lessons.excerpt: neither authenticated encryption nor I/O is a bottleneck by itself, but their naive combination is.

lessons.point: Rollback protection needs a separate mechanism because the hardware offers none.
lessons.excerpt: CVMs lack hardware primitives for this purpose, requiring alternative solutions.

entries.takeaway: Running in a confidential VM does not protect data on disk; stored data needs its own integrity and rollback protection.

actionable.title: Check what protects data at rest in confidential VMs
actionable.detail: For workloads in confidential VMs, confirm that disks use authenticated encryption with keys held inside the VM, and decide how you detect a provider rolling storage back to an older state, since the hardware gives no freshness guarantee.

entries.verify_note: Faithful to the abstract; figures are the authors' own, for large objects, and freshness is eventual due to epoch batching.
entries.prior_art: Disk encryption and integrity layers inside confidential VMs and trusted-counter rollback defenses exist; the paper's claim is near-raw throughput from co-designing the input/output path.
entries.threat: A cloud provider reading, altering or rolling back a confidential workload's persistent data.
entries.conditions: Stateful workloads in confidential VMs whose storage sits outside the trust boundary.
entries.mitigations: Authenticated encryption of stored data with keys inside the VM, plus an external trusted counter for freshness.

entries.title: ESET: UAC-0099 used MythicRatatoskr with C2 inside Yggdrasil before Sandworm struck
entries.summary: ESET found that UAC-0099 broke into a Ukrainian logistics company by spear-phishing in July 2025 and later deployed a new backdoor called MythicRatatoskr. Its command-and-control (C2) server sits inside Yggdrasil, an experimental peer-to-peer mesh network, which ESET calls the first documented state-aligned abuse of it. Access was handed to Sandworm, which wiped data two months later by pushing SDelete through Active Directory Group Policy.

lessons.point: C2 hosted inside a peer-to-peer mesh overlay is a new resilience and stealth tactic for state actors.
lessons.excerpt: UAC-0099's use of a previously undocumented backdoor called MythicRatatoskr that communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server hosted inside the Yggdrasil mesh network.

lessons.point: A 10-minute startup delay postpones the first Yggdrasil connection to evade detection.
lessons.excerpt: some artifacts include a 10-minute startup delay in a likely effort to avoid immediately connecting to the Yggdrasil network and evade detection.

lessons.point: The destructive stage used a legitimate tool pushed via domain Group Policy, not custom wiper code.

entries.title: Chainguard Athena agents deduplicate private zero-day reports without leaking reporters
entries.summary: Chainguard describes the pipeline behind Athena, which it says has validated 21,175 zero-days in open-source packages. Fingerprints (package, method, weakness type) and embedding similarity were not reliable for deduplication, so an agent now reads the source and compares each new report against existing records. Validation code, not the agent, writes the records. An enrichment agent traces the vulnerable behavior through Git history and release branches to find the affected range, because fixes often land in silent refactors or as backports with different commits. A second agent reviews proposed fix boundaries in an isolated microVM with no credentials or network access. Separate checks strip submitter-identifying details and require a summary, a confirmed code location and a CVSS vector before a record is saved.
entries.takeaway: Version ranges, duplicate decisions and fixed-version claims in a vulnerability database are each judgments that can be wrong; keep agents advisory and let deterministic validation own the writes.

lessons.point: Deduplication must compare the defect and the code responsible, not just affected versions or matching fields.
lessons.excerpt: Affected-version overlap alone is insufficient: separate vulnerabilities can affect the same versions, and a duplicate report can identify an affected version we have not recorded yet.

lessons.point: Fix-boundary analysis has to read code changes, because silent fixes hide in refactors.
lessons.excerpt: Commit messages are not enough, as an ordinary refactor can remove a vulnerability without mentioning security.

lessons.point: Agents propose decisions; validation code applies them, so a bad output cannot mint IDs or overwrite records.
lessons.excerpt: The agent cannot create identifiers or update records directly.

lessons.point: A CVE alias and a fix are separate facts; mapping to an advisory does not mean a remediation exists.
lessons.excerpt: Adding an alias does not establish that a fix is available.

actionable.title: Treat fixed-version and duplicate decisions as evidence-backed judgments in your own vuln pipeline
actionable.detail: If you run internal vulnerability triage with LLM agents: have the agent return decision plus rationale only, and let validation code write records; process each package's submissions one at a time to avoid racing duplicate checks; keep merged records as withdrawn aliases; never let a range update reclassify a confirmed-fixed version as affected (or drop a confirmed-vulnerable one) without resolving the conflict; and verify version-to-commit mappings against registry and repository history rather than trusting commit messages.

entries.verify_note: Excerpts verbatim; vendor process post with no accuracy data. Novelty lowered to the verifier's 35.
entries.prior_art: Earlier Chainguard posts in the archive (Athena harness and silent-fix disclosure, 'Patching a vulnerability that has no fix', the Black Duck OSV feed) cover finding and patching. OSV.dev already computes affected ranges from Git commit history. New here: the record-building layer for private reports, including agent-based deduplication after fingerprint and embedding matching fell short, a second-agent fix-boundary review, submitter-confidentiality scrubbing, and invariants on range updates. It is a vendor process description with no accuracy numbers.

entries.title: Pillow EPS handling lets attacker-controlled filenames inject Ghostscript arguments (GHSA-w889-685w-c8fh)
entries.summary: The advisory reports that Pillow's EPS plugin builds the Ghostscript command line from the input file's name with no sanitization. Tested on 12.3.0; the suggested fix is to normalize the path to an absolute path.

lessons.excerpt: it is not mitigated by Pillow's default -dSAFER setting.

lessons.point: The fix is to normalize the path so it can never parse as an option.
lessons.excerpt: Normalize the filename to an absolute path before it is passed to Ghostscript

entries.title: Wiz scans every new npm version at publish time to catch compromises
entries.summary: Wiz describes a pipeline that analyzes each new npm package version as soon as it is published. entries.title: Blockchain analysts tie record Binance hot-wallet theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor
entries.summary: Attackers took about $6.3 billion from Binance hot wallets across ten blockchains on October 29, and most of it left within about 20 minutes. Binance's early findings point to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop that gave access to a service container able to submit withdrawals. TRM Labs judges that the attacker could make Binance's hot-wallet signing system sign any transaction it chose. TRM attributes the theft to the North Korean unit TraderTraitor with high confidence.

lessons.point: Binance's early findings point to one engineer's laptop reaching a service container that could submit withdrawals, and it found no evidence of a private key leak.
lessons.excerpt: may involve a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions

lessons.point: If attackers can drive the signing system, protecting the keys is not enough. Valid signatures across different chains and key types point to abuse of the signer itself.
lessons.excerpt: the most likely explanation is that the attacker gained the ability to make Binance’s hot wallet signing system sign transactions of its choosing across chains

lessons.point: On Ethereum the attackers used EIP-7702 delegation. They pre-signed a batch of permissions so that one would match the wallet's transaction count (nonce) when it ran.
lessons.excerpt: They sent a batch of 50 such permissions, all signed beforehand by a Binance hot wallet, so that one would match the wallet’s transaction count at execution time.

lessons.point: Fast freezes by token issuers held back a large share, but the ETH and BTC the attackers kept have no issuer that can freeze them.
lessons.excerpt: By 00:30 UTC on October 30, TRM tallied around $2.7 billion in frozen assets

entries.takeaway: The signing service, and every container and engineer laptop that can submit requests to it, is the real security boundary for hot wallets. Protecting the keys does not help once an attacker can ask the signer to sign.

actionable.title: Put independent policy checks in front of transaction-signing services
actionable.detail: Make the signer enforce its own limits on withdrawal value, rate and destination before it signs. Require a second approval path that service containers reachable from engineer laptops cannot satisfy. Alert when wallets sign across several chains in a short burst, and when EIP-7702 delegation authorizations are signed from hot wallets.

entries.verify_note: Verifier: mostly supported; 'no private key was stolen' and the native-coin freeze point overreached Binance's hedged early findings, reworded. Novelty lowered to the verifier's 40.
entries.prior_art: The pool has no crypto-exchange heist or TraderTraitor entry. The nearest DPRK items are the archive Axios npm compromise attributed to Sapphire Sleet and a DPRK-linked PHP scanning mention in product-security, both unrelated attack paths. This is a news synthesis of TRM Labs and Binance statements with little technical detail on the signer compromise.
entries.threat: A state-sponsored actor compromises a DevOps engineer's laptop, reaches a service container that can submit withdrawals, and makes the hot-wallet signing system sign attacker transactions across ten chains. On Ethereum it also abuses pre-signed EIP-7702 delegations.
entries.conditions: Hot-wallet signing can be triggered from service containers reachable from engineer endpoints, and the signer has no independent check on value, rate or destination for withdrawals.
entries.mitigations: Isolate signing services from DevOps endpoints. Make the signer enforce withdrawal policy and require out-of-band approval. Monitor for burst signing across chains and for EIP-7702 delegation signatures. Line up rapid-freeze contacts with stablecoin issuers ahead of time.

entries.prior_art: Many prior Pillow decompression-bomb and parser-hang DoS advisories; the inherited-method/overridden-tell() root cause is a routine variation.
entries.title: Pillow DoS: a 5.6 KB MIC file hangs n_frames
entries.summary: A crafted 5.6 KB Microsoft Image Composer file makes Pillow loop forever at 100% CPU when code reads im.n_frames, on installs with the optional olefile package. MicImageFile overrides seek() and tell() but inherits TiffImageFile.n_frames, which relies on tell() advancing, so it re-parses the same directory endlessly. The hang raises no exception and grows no memory; the regression dates to Pillow 7.2.0 (2020).

lessons.point: Exposure depends on an optional dependency: only installs with olefile register the MIC plugin.
lessons.excerpt: This only affects installations that have the optional `olefile` package.

lessons.point: Root cause is a subclass that overrides the primitives an inherited method depends on; audit inherited methods when you change seek/tell semantics.
lessons.excerpt: It does not override the `n_frames` property, so the inherited TIFF implementation runs

lessons.point: Silent CPU hangs evade exception handlers and memory limits; untrusted parsing needs a wall-clock watchdog.
lessons.excerpt: The call never returns, raises no exception, and does not grow memory, so only an external watchdog stops it.

lessons.point: The bug has shipped since Pillow 7.2.0.
lessons.excerpt: first released in 7.2.0

entries.takeaway: Affects installs with olefile, back to Pillow 7.2.0. Parse untrusted images under a timeout and restrict Image.open to the formats you expect.

actionable.title: Bound untrusted image parsing
actionable.detail: Pass an explicit formats= allowlist to Image.open for user uploads, drop olefile if you don't need MIC/FPX, and run frame-count and re-save operations in a worker with a wall-clock timeout.

entries.threat: Denial of service: one crafted upload pins a worker at 100% CPU indefinitely.
entries.conditions: olefile installed; the application opens an untrusted image and reads n_frames (e.g. is-animated checks, save_all re-saves).
entries.mitigations: Upgrade Pillow when patched; restrict formats; remove olefile; enforce worker timeouts.

editorial.reason: Fresh HIGH advisory in Pillow, which nearly every Python upload path uses; the fix pattern (formats allowlist, drop olefile, wall-clock timeouts) applies today.

entries.title: raml-kql runs one KQL query across workspaces without a Defender multi-tenant org
entries.author: Luca Ramseyer

lessons.point: The design keeps no credentials of its own: it acts only with the user's delegated permissions.
lessons.excerpt: Raml KQL only ever does what you are allowed to do: it uses your delegated permissions and holds no secrets or service principals.

lessons.point: It records query provenance without storing customer data.
lessons.excerpt: A hash-chained audit log records what ran where, without result values.

lessons.point: Customer names are masked by default for screen sharing.
lessons.excerpt: Tenant and workspace names are aliased on screen by default
